catalogTitle: סעודת "טוב להודות לה'"

oneLiner.en: At a Purim Katan seudah the Mashgiach explains why the fourteenth of Adar I still calls for a commemoration of the miracle, and why Purim's high light needs to be repeated and strengthened, ending with 'Tov lehodos laShem', the good of praising Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah that Adar I and Adar II differ only in Megillah reading and gifts to the poor, and the dispute whether feasting is required on Adar I, which the Rema settles with 'increase the meal a little'. With the Magen Avraham's rule on commemorating a miracle, he asks how such a commemoration could be pushed off entirely. He brings the Chasam Sofer, who says the Torah-level duty to commemorate a miracle is met in Adar I by refraining from eulogy and fasting, and questions it. He weighs zerizus against doing a mitzvah in its finest way, and explains 'igeres haPurim hashenis'. From Pharaoh's doubled dream and the Maharal he explains that Purim's light comes from so high that it must be repeated to stay in the world, and that a leap year needs two Purims. He closes with 'Tov lehodos laShem' and brachos.

en: According to the Mashgiach, beyond the Purim that Mordechai and Esther instituted, there is a general duty, as the Magen Avraham writes, to commemorate a miracle, and this is why something of Purim remains on Adar I.
The Mashgiach explains the Rema's 'increase the meal a little' as adding wine, since the Purim seudah requires wine while a general commemoration of a miracle does not.

The Mashgiach questions the Chasam Sofer's view that refraining from eulogy and fasting fulfils the commemoration, since a commemoration must be a positive act, and on an ordinary day too there is no eulogy or fast.
Purim's miracle came from so high a place, beyond nature and beyond understanding, that its light tends to rise back up, so it must be held and strengthened by repetition.
This repetition, the Mashgiach suggests, is behind reading the Megillah at night and again by day, and behind Esther's making two feasts.
In a leap year the lowliness of the thirteenth month is deeper still, so two Purims are needed, Purim Katan together with the great Purim.
The Purim Katan seudah is an expression of 'Tov lehodos laShem': it is good to praise Hashem, and a person who has a taste in davening finds that all of his life changes.

title.en: Feasting on Adar I and the Rema

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah on Adar I and II and the dispute over feasting on Adar I, settled by the Rema. With the Magen Avraham's rule on commemorating a miracle, he asks how Adar I can be left empty, and explains the Rema's 'increase a little' as adding wine.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer and the Mashgiach's question

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Chasam Sofer close to what he once said: commemorating a miracle is a Torah duty, fulfilled in Adar I by refraining from eulogy and fasting. He then asks how refraining can be a commemoration, when a positive act is needed.

title.en: Zerizus, mitzvah min hamuvchar and 'hashenis'

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests the dispute may follow Rav Nachman and Rava on Hallel, then weighs zerizus against a mitzvah in its finest form, with the Chacham Tzvi and the Terumas HaDeshen. He explains how zerizus applies to Purim and how 'igeres haPurim hashenis' refers to reading the Megillah a second time.

title.en: Purim's high light must be repeated

summary.en: From a case of mistaken Kiddush the Mashgiach shows that Adar I holds some holiness of Purim. With Pharaoh's doubled dream and the Maharal he explains that Purim's light comes from so high that it must be strengthened by repetition, as in reading the Megillah twice and Esther's two feasts.

title.en: Two Purims, 'Tov lehodos' and brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the thirteenth month is a deeper darkness that needs a double Purim, and that the seudah is a commemoration and a preparation for the next Purim. He speaks on 'Tov lehodos laShem' and the taste of good davening, and closes with brachos for salvation and the final redemption.

catalogTitle: The Great Effect of Tekias Shofar. The נסיון of עקידת יצחק as Applicable to our Generation

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Akeidah was a test of serving Hashem while He seems far away and full of contradictions, that our generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha lives through that same test, and that the shofar we received from the Akeidah disperses the clouds and renews the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar's picture of the end of the year: the bounty allotted last Rosh Hashanah is used up, and clouds separate Hashem from Knesses Yisrael. Our earthly shofar arouses the heavenly shofar, disperses the clouds and draws down new bounty, and with the hundred sounds and the verses of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances. To explain this he turns to the Akeidah. Nisayon also means raising up. Why was the Akeidah, a direct command from Hashem, the hardest test? The Zohar answers that Avraham saw Hashem from afar: the command contradicted the promise about Yitzchak, and he obeyed without understanding. Following the Ramban that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Mashgiach teaches that the last generation before Moshiach, the heel of Adam's body, faces this same test of confusion. Avraham's emunah reaching down to the heel gives us the strength to hold on, and the ram of the Akeidah gave us the shofar.

en: At the end of the year the bounty is used up and clouds separate Hashem from Klal Yisrael; the shofar disperses them and draws down new bounty for the coming year.
Through the shofar and the ten verses of each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances.
The test of the Akeidah was that Hashem's command contradicted His promise about Yitzchak, and Avraham obeyed while confused and without understanding.
Since the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha must pass the test of the Akeidah: emunah amid questions and hester panim.
Avraham's emunah reached down to the heel, and that gives his children the strength to keep emunah in the hardest conditions; emunah will never leave Klal Yisrael.
The shofar of Rosh Hashanah comes from the ram of the Akeidah, and it renews both the calendar year and, at the end of days, the whole world.
Even when Hashem seems distant, His love for Klal Yisrael is not extinguished; He loves them even more because He sees their struggle.

title.en: The shofar disperses the year-end clouds

summary.en: Following the Zohar, the Mashgiach describes how the bounty of the past year runs out and clouds come between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. The earthly shofar arouses the heavenly shofar, disperses the clouds and brings new bounty, and with the hundred sounds and the verses of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances.

title.en: Nisayon as raising up; the first test and the last

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the Akeidah, explains that nisayon also means raising up, like a child promoted after a test, and describes Avraham's first test in Ur Kasdim, where he gave his life for a G-d who had never spoken to him. He asks why the Akeidah, commanded by Hashem Himself, should be harder.

title.en: He saw the Makom from afar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar on 'he saw the place from afar': Avraham saw Hashem as distant, because the command to bring Yitzchak contradicted the promise that his offspring would come through Yitzchak, and Hashem does not change His mind. Avraham refused to dwell on the question and obeyed blindly.

title.en: Why Avraham could not see the answer

summary.en: Through Rashi, the Mashgiach shows that the answer was simple: Hashem had said to bring Yitzchak up, not to slaughter him. Avraham did not see it because a test means the answers are hidden; this is hester panim, which can come on a person or a generation, and Avraham told the Satan he would not listen to him.

title.en: The deeds of the Avos as a sign for the children

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's rule that whatever happened to the Avos foreshadows their children, illustrated by Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim. It follows that Klal Yisrael must pass ten tests, and the last one, before Moshiach, is the Akeidah's test of a clouded mind and a heart without feeling.

title.en: Malachi: believers in the last generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Malachi, the last prophet, describes the generation before Moshiach saying that serving Hashem does not pay, yet promises that those who fear Hashem will gather and strengthen one another. As Avraham held on to emunah, a backbone of believers will remain, and the Medrash says they will rejoice more over keeping their emunah than over the Geulah itself.

title.en: Our questions and the heel of Adam

summary.en: The Mashgiach says our generation is full of questions on Hashem, which are easy to answer only after the test. Every generation corresponds to a limb of Adam's body, and the last generation is the heel, which has no feeling. At the Akeidah Avraham was transported into this condition, and Hashem's blessing 'eikev asher shamata' alludes to it.

title.en: The Akeidah fulfilled the promise

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar, the Mashgiach explains that Yitzchak could not have children before the Akeidah; there his neshamah left him and returned with an addition, so that right afterward Rivkah's birth is told. The Akeidah, which seemed to cancel the promise, actually fulfilled it, and what seems bad to a person with emunah turns out to be for his good.

title.en: Emes, the last word of Shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that today Hashem is distant and this is our tafkid in a world of kefirah. The 248 words of Shema correspond to the 248 limbs; the first word is the head and the last, emes, is the heel, and in ikvesa d'Meshicha the Gemara says emes will be missing, so one must believe in it in the dark.

title.en: Chavakuk's one mitzvah: emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that later generations concentrated the 613 mitzvos, until Chavakuk stood the whole Torah on emunah, because small generations cannot put full effort into every mitzvah. Pure emunah is hard today, but because Avraham's emunah reached the heel, emunah is eternal in Klal Yisrael and gives us strength now.

title.en: Moshiach girded with tzedakah and emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Moshiach pleading to come while the Satan accuses, and says he will prevail with the strength of tzedakah and emunah, which are inseparable, as the passuk in Yeshayah calls them the belt of his loins. He urges strengthening emunah and learning sefarim that strengthen it.

title.en: The ram of the Akeidah and Shema Yisrael

summary.en: Returning to the opening, the Mashgiach explains that at the Akeidah Avraham dispersed the clouds of confusion and his emunah was renewed, and from the ram caught by its horns we received the shofar, which renews the world each year. Rosh Hashanah is the head of the year as emunah is the head of the mitzvos; Shema Yisrael, the last verse of Malchiyos, equals 'shofar shel ayil' in gematria, and the Gemara says the kingship is accepted through the shofar.

title.en: The year as a miniature of world history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the year is a miniature of the world's whole history, which ends at the end of days and begins again. Bereishis hints at 'bara tayish', the ram created at the beginning for Avraham, so the world begins with the strength of the shofar, and the new world will also begin with the great shofar. Today the universal year is at its end, covered with thick clouds.

title.en: Birth pangs of Moshiach and Hashem's love

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares our time to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor, matching the seventy words of Lamnatzeach that end with 'b'yom kareinu', where we stand now. Malachi opens with 'I have loved you', and the haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah says Hashem appears from afar with eternal love; the hardship is for our good like the Akeidah. He closes with a brachah for teshuvah sheleimah and the great shofar.

catalogTitle: עיקר הפורים הוא בעקבתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the main Purim has not yet come: it is the last Purim before Moshiach, in the time of greatest hiddenness, and from Purim Katan a Jew draws the strength not to be afraid.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rema that one should add a little feasting on Purim Katan, and with the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi that the main Purim is in the first Adar, which is ruled so in a heichal in Heaven, from where light descends today. He then explains why reading the Megillah 'backwards' does not fulfil the mitzvah: Purim is not only a past event, since the main Purim, the complete wiping out of Amalek, comes in the hiddenness before Moshiach. He brings the Sfas Emes that another Purim may precede the third Beis Hamikdash, and describes Haman's kelipah as fear. He connects the Babylon of his day and Achashverosh's rule 'by himself' to that last Purim, tells how Chizkiyahu slept calmly on Pesach night, and brings Mordechai and the children's pesukim against fear. He ends with Purim Katan as the last siman of Orach Chaim, accepting Torah anew, and an appeal for a hachnasas orchim.

en: According to the Mashgiach, the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi that Purim belongs in the first Adar is upheld in a heichal in Heaven, and its light reaches us on Purim Katan.
Unlike Pesach and Shavuos, the main Purim has not yet happened: the full wiping out of Amalek comes in the hiddenness before Moshiach.
The closer to the end of days, the greater the hiddenness, and therefore the greater the Purim; in every generation Amalek wages a new war, and so there is a new Purim.
Haman's kelipah is fear: he did nothing but cast fear on the Jews, and the Megillah teaches not to be overcome by that fear.
The Mashgiach says one should say every day, especially nowadays, the three pesukim the children told Mordechai, which teach not to fear.
The laws of Purim Katan are the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, matching Adar as the last month and the time before Moshiach.

the war with Amalek in every generation

title.en: Purim Katan and the heichal in Heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rema on feasting on Purim Katan and the Gemara's dispute whether Purim belongs in the first or second Adar. He explains that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi's view is ruled in a heichal in Heaven, from where light comes down today, and introduces the sefarim's reading of 'one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled his obligation'.

title.en: The main Purim is still to come

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Purim with Pesach and Shavuos: their events are past and their light returns each year, but the main Purim, the complete wiping out of Amalek, has not yet been. He ties Purim to the hiddenness of 'haster astir', which the Torah places at the end of days, and explains that every generation has a new war with Amalek and so a new Purim.

title.en: A Purim before the third Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sfas Emes that just as the Purim miracle gave the Jews the uplift to build the second Beis Hamikdash, there may be another such miracle before Moshiach. On this he explains 'reading the Megillah backwards': one who thinks Purim is only past misses that the real Purim is just before Moshiach, and he brings the Ya'avetz on the miracle of Jewish survival in exile.

title.en: Haman's fear and the Babylon of today

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Haman's kelipah as fear and says Amalek in this generation is clothed in Babylon, whose ruler claims to be Nebuchadnezzar and threatens the Jews. He brings the Rashab's writings on the seventy nations' ministering angels, the passuk 'kol kli yutzar alayich lo yitzlach', and the Shabbos zemer's request that Babylon too be crushed.

title.en: The first petichta and a king 'by himself'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the first petichta of the Midrash on the Megillah speaks of cutting off Babylon, and answers that the last Purim before Moshiach is the Purim of 'v'hikrati l'Vavel'. In a lighter Purim vein he explains Achashverosh as a king who ruled 'by himself', chosen by Hashem and not by the people, compares it to the Maharal on the giving of the Torah, and applies it to the American president of his day.

title.en: Chizkiyahu's sleep and the children's pesukim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Chizkiyahu slept calmly on Pesach night while Sancheriv's army surrounded Yerushalayim, a sign of bitachon. He explains that Purim's 'v'nahafoch' turns fear back onto the enemy, brings 'tipol aleihem eimasa vafachad' and the passuk about Yishmael, and tells how Mordechai was encouraged by the pesukim the children told him, which the Mashgiach says one should say daily.

title.en: The last siman of Orach Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the laws of Purim Katan are the last siman of Orach Chaim, 697, and brings the Ya'avetz that the Mechaber numbered the simanim with ruach hakodesh. He offers gematrias on the number and calls for a renewed acceptance of Torah, as in 'kiymu v'kiblu'.

title.en: Hachnasas orchim and closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises a hachnasas orchim founded by Rabbi Boruch Halberstam in Boro Park and asks the listeners to help it. He closes with the Rema's last halacha in Orach Chaim on feasting on Purim Katan and a brachah for the full wiping out of Amalek and the building of the third Beis Hamikdash.

catalogTitle: אביגיל מלכת פורים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Gemara tells the story of Avigail in the middle of the laws of Purim: Avigail, whose name equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, is the aspect of Purim, the beginning of the kingdom of the house of David, which is completed through Bas Sheva and Pesach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach retells how Avigail stopped David from killing Naval, telling him 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah', which the Gemara counts as prophecy, hinting at Bas Sheva. He asks what kind of prophecy that is, and why the story stands in the Purim sugya. Bringing the Gemara that Mordechai's yom tov was not accepted, he says that the Megillah speaks on two levels, the historical Achashverosh and the King, Hashem, and of the final war with Amalek; the full yom tov still waits. He explains the Bas Sheva episode: David knew she was his zivug, and the kingdom of David must come through hidden, talked-about ways so the Satan will not notice. Avigail, from the same root, saw that David thought Moshiach would come from her and told him: not through me. Avigail equals Esther Hamalkah; Purim is the start of the kingdom, completed at Pesach. He closes with the simcha of Purim Katan.

en: The Gemara counts Avigail's words 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah' as prophecy, because they hinted at the episode of Bas Sheva.
The Megillah speaks on two levels: the historical Achashverosh, and the King, Hashem, and the final war with Amalek; therefore the yom tov Mordechai wanted was not yet accepted.
The kingdom of the house of David comes through hidden ways that cause people to talk, so that the Satan will not realize where it is coming from; this is why David acted as he did with Bas Sheva.
Avigail understood that David thought Moshiach would come from her, and told him that the kingdom would come through Bas Sheva and not through her.
Avigail is the aspect of Purim and of Esther; Purim is the beginning of the kingdom of the house of David and of the redemption, which continues to Pesach.
On Purim Katan there is no Megillah, mishloach manos or matanos la'evyonim, but the mitzvah of simcha applies.

title.en: Opening

summary.en: The opening of the shiur.

title.en: The story of Avigail, Naval and David

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells how David, fleeing Shaul, asked Naval for food, how Avigail stopped him from killing Naval, and how she told him 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah'. He brings the Gemara that this was prophecy, hinting at the episode of Bas Sheva.

title.en: Why this story in the Purim sugya; the Megillah's two levels

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara tells this story at length in the laws of Purim, and what kind of prophecy Avigail's words were. He brings the Gemara that Mordechai's yom tov was not accepted, and explains that the Megillah speaks both of the historical Achashverosh and of the King, Hashem, and the final war with Amalek, so the yom tov is not yet complete.

title.en: David and Bas Sheva: the hidden root of the kingdom

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the episode of Bas Sheva could happen to David, who learned from Shmuel and never separated from Hashem. He brings that David saw in prophecy that she was his zivug, and explains that the Satan fears the kingdom of David, so it comes through hidden ways that cause talk, as with Rus.

title.en: David caused the talk; the fast for the fast

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David deliberately caused people to talk, yet still needed atonement, like one who fasts on Shabbos and needs a fast for that fast, or the nazir who brings a chatas. He then explains that David understood Avigail was his zivug, from the same root as Bas Sheva.

title.en: Hod, Purim to Pesach, and Avigail's answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the kingdom comes from the aspect of hod, that Purim is the beginning of the kingdom of David and leads to Pesach, and that Avigail told David: not through me, the kingdom will come from Bas Sheva. He adds that Purim prepares the three mitzvos of a king, Amalek and the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Avigail equals Esther Hamalkah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Avigail the wife of David equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, and that a missing yud in her name shows that malchus is missing. He explains that Avigail is the aspect of Purim, and connects the first place each name appears in the pesukim.

title.en: The simcha of Purim Katan and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim Katan only the mitzvah of simcha remains, ties it to the end of the Shulchan Aruch and to Haman's lot falling in the first Adar, and closes with a brachah to be together in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ב - עושים שמחה כדי לזכור הנס

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why, although the custom is not to make a full feast on Purim Katan, a Jew should still rejoice that day: the miracle must be remembered, and on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rema's ruling on Purim Katan: some hold one must make a feast, the custom is not so, yet one should add somewhat to the meal, for 'a good heart is a constant feast'. He brings the Magen Avraham that every miracle obligates a yearly celebration, learned by kal vachomer from Hallel, and argues that by 'ein maavirin al hamitzvos' and 'zichru nifle'osav' it should belong to the first Adar. The Anshei Knesses HaGedolah set Purim in the second Adar, but the first still carries the mitzvah of remembering. Purim has two laws, the feast for the miracle and the wine instituted by Mordechai and Esther, which Purim Katan lacks. Finally he explains that on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, as Boaz's 'vayitav libo' refers to Torah study, so a Jew should rejoice on Purim Katan.

en: The Rema writes that some obligate a feast on Purim Katan and the custom is not so, yet one should add somewhat to the meal, since 'a good heart is a constant feast'.
According to the Magen Avraham, every miracle that happens to Jews obligates a yearly celebration, learned by kal vachomer from the Gemara's reasoning about saying Hallel.
Because of 'ein maavirin al hamitzvos' and the duty to remember Hashem's wonders within the year, the celebration of the miracle seemingly belongs on Purim Katan in the first Adar.

Purim has two separate laws: a feast to celebrate the miracle, and drinking wine as a remembrance, instituted by Mordechai and Esther because the miracle came through wine; the second does not apply to Purim Katan.
On Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, and a Jew cannot fail to rejoice over this on Purim Katan as well.
The simcha of Torah is not tied to a set day, so the custom of not making a feast on Purim Katan does not exclude rejoicing in the Torah on that day.

title.en: The Rema and the Magen Avraham on Purim Katan

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents the Rema's ruling that the custom is not to make a feast on Purim Katan, yet one should add somewhat to the meal. He brings the Magen Avraham that a miracle must be celebrated every year, derived by kal vachomer from Hallel, and notes that because of 'ein maavirin al hamitzvos' it would belong in the first Adar.

title.en: Remembering the miracle and the two laws of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the duty of 'zichru nifle'osav' to reading Parshas Zachor every year so that it is not forgotten, which would seemingly require a feast on Purim Katan. He then distinguishes two laws of Purim, the feast for the miracle and the wine instituted by Mordechai and Esther, and uses this to explain the Rema's wording.

title.en: Purim Katan and the joy of accepting the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Purim Katan is and answers that on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, a joy no Jew can postpone. He brings Boaz's 'vayitav libo', which the Gemara explains as Torah study, and concludes that rejoicing in the Torah belongs to every day and surely to Purim Katan, ending with a wish for joy in Heaven and the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Recreating the World through מלכיות זכרונות שופרות; תקיעת שופר

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Rosh Hashanah the creation of Adam and the world is truly repeated, and that through the shofar and the pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros each Jew returns to his pure root and becomes a partner in re-creating the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that Hashem blew the breath of life into Adam: blowing comes from a person's very insides, more than speech. Since shanah means repetition, he compares the year to a rotary file: when Rosh Hashanah comes around, Adam is created anew, and with the shofar we blow that breath back to Hashem. As at the first creation, angels argue each year whether man should be re-created. But every Jew has a hidden point that wants Hashem's will, as the Rambam explains about one who is coerced until he says he wants. This point is the level of Bereishis, the first of the ten utterances, which is above speech; from it comes the atonement of Yom Kippur, and the shofar speaks to Hashem from there without words. Hashem makes each Jew a partner in re-creating his part of the world through the ten pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros. Finally, the shofar is the sound of return, like the Yovel.

en: Hashem blew the breath of life into Adam, and blowing comes from a person's innermost being, deeper than speech.
Shanah means repetition, so each Rosh Hashanah the creation of Adam truly happens again, not just as a remembrance.
In the depth of his heart every Jew, even a rasha, wants to do Hashem's will; this point is beyond words and beyond the angels' grasp.
The shofar speaks to Hashem from the level that precedes speech, the level of Bereishis, where no sin reaches.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem gives every Jew the task of re-creating the world, through the ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros.
Rosh Hashanah is a return to the root, like the Yovel, and the shofar is the sound of that return.

title.en: The breath of life blown back each year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'vayipach' means Hashem blew the soul into Adam from His innermost. Since shanah means repetition, he pictures the year as a rotary file of days, so that each Rosh Hashanah Adam is truly created anew, and with the shofar we blow that breath back to Hashem.

title.en: The angels debate man's creation every year

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Hashem consulted the angels before creating Adam, some for and some against, and those against were cast down to this world. Since the year repeats, every Rosh Hashanah angels again argue whether each person deserves another year.

title.en: The hidden point that wants Hashem's will

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the angels cannot grasp the Jewish neshamah: in every Jew is a hidden point, beyond words, that does not want to sin. He brings the Gemara that one who refuses to bring a korban is coerced until he says 'I want', and the Rambam's explanation that the coercion only subdues the body and the yetzer hara so the real inner will comes out.

title.en: Bereishis, the tenth level above speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes ten levels of holiness up to the Kodesh HaKodashim, where the Kohen Gadol gains atonement on Yom Kippur. He brings the Gemara that 'Bereishis' is also one of the ten utterances, and the Maggid of Mezritch's explanation that it is above speech; there every Jew's pure neshamah wants no sin, and from there comes Yom Kippur's atonement.

title.en: The shofar: speaking without words

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the shofar speaks to Hashem from the inner breath before it is formed into words, the level where no sin reaches, and that this inner will declared on Rosh Hashanah is revealed on Yom Kippur. He then explains why the makri does not announce the very first tekiah: not because of a hefsek, but because words are not yet created.

title.en: Re-creating the world with ten pesukim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem tells every Jew to create the world anew on Rosh Hashanah through teshuvah and tefillah, with ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros paralleling the ten utterances, and a hundred sounds. As 'na'aseh adam' shows, man is a partner, and like the generation of the Mabul each person's deeds shape his part of the world; he urges saying the pesukim with full kavanah.

title.en: Shofar and Yovel: returning to the root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the law of return: in the Yovel, the fiftieth year, everyone goes back to his land, and the fiftieth day after Pesach was Matan Torah with the shofar. From the burning of the Beis HaMikdash on the tenth of Av until Rosh Hashanah is fifty days, so the shofar of Rosh Hashanah is the sound of returning to Hashem. He closes with wishes for a good Rosh Hashanah.

catalogTitle: תש"ס - אפשר כשיבא משיח יהיה פורים באדר ראשון

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, following the Chasam Sofer, that placing Purim next to Nissan is a segulah for salvation needed in galus, and suggests that when Moshiach comes Purim of a leap year may move to Adar Rishon, the month that repairs the diminished moon.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Yerushalmi that Adar Rishon is an addition and Adar Sheni the main month, and then brings the Gemara's dispute over which Adar of a leap year holds Purim: Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi argues from 'one does not pass over mitzvos', Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from joining redemption to redemption. He asks what lies behind the second reason, which Rashi gives no verse for. From the Chasam Sofer's account of how Haman and the Sanhedrin calculated the year, he concludes that joining the redemptions is a segulah for salvation, not a halacha. In galus Jews need that segulah like bread; when Moshiach comes it will no longer be needed, so Purim may then fall in Adar Rishon. He explains the name Purim Katan through the small luminary and the moon's diminution, which Adar Rishon repairs, and closes with the humility of Shaul, Mordechai and Esther.

en: Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi places Purim of a leap year in the first Adar because one does not pass over mitzvos; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel places it in the second to join the redemption of Adar to that of Nissan, and the practice follows him.
From the Chasam Sofer's account of Haman's calculation the Mashgiach concludes that joining redemption to redemption is a segulah for salvation, neither a Torah law nor a rabbinic one.
In galus Jews need Purim's power of salvation like bread, so the Sages fixed it in the second Adar; when Moshiach comes that need falls away and Purim may move to Adar Rishon.
The name Purim Katan points to the small luminary: Adar Rishon is the month that fills in the moon's diminution and reconciles Kenesses Yisrael with Hashem.
Humility brings kingship and salvation: Binyamin, Shaul and Mordechai had lowliness in themselves, and Esther, like the moon, had nothing of her own.

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Yerushalmi that Adar Rishon is an addition, then sets out the Gemara's dispute between Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi (one does not pass over mitzvos) and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (join redemption to redemption). He asks what the root of the second reason is, that it can override the first.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: Haman's calculation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's derush: Haman picked a year that should have been a leap year so his Adar would be far from Nissan, and the Sanhedrin countered by making it a plain year. From this he proves that joining redemption to redemption is a segulah, which the Sages kept because the days are remembered and re-enacted.

title.en: When Moshiach comes: Purim in Adar Rishon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in galus Jews need Purim's salvation like bread, against the power of Achashverosh, through the power of Mordechai and against Haman. When Moshiach comes it will only be a remembrance, so only the reason of not passing over mitzvos remains, and he suggests Purim of a leap year will then be in Adar Rishon.

title.en: Purim Katan and the diminished moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the day is called Purim Katan and not Purim Rishon, and answers that Adar Rishon repairs the moon's diminution, the root of a chain of jealousies through history. Esther is the moon, and he ends with a brachah that in the merit of Purim Katan every Jew should long to reconcile with Hashem.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Lowliness brings kingship and redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who has lowliness in himself merits kingship: Binyamin, Shaul, who did not reveal his kingship, and Mordechai, of whom it is said that Hashem stands at the right of the poor. Esther, like the moon, had nothing of her own, and the redemption came through people of true humility, upon whom Hashem looks.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ו - שמחים בנקודה קטנה שבתוך יהודי

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim Jews rejoice with the small hidden point in every Jew, the root that milah binds without da'as and from which mesiras nefesh comes.

abstract.en: Near the end of the seudah of Purim Katan, the Mashgiach notes that the seudah is not obligatory by law, yet Jews rejoice with the Ribono shel Olam and His miracles, fulfilling the Rema's closing words in Shulchan Aruch. He then explains matanos la'evyonim through the saying that true poverty is poverty in da'as. He contrasts Amalek, the worst klipah, with milah, the covenant of Avraham Avinu, and asks why milah is not delayed until the child can do it with intent. His answer: precisely without da'as the infant is bound to the hidden root of the Jewish people. On Purim one rejoices with this hidden point, the love one does not even feel. Milah, without da'as, and tefillin, which demand constant da'as, belong together, and Purim joins them. From the root above da'as comes mesiras nefesh, which Hashem's decree drew out of Mordechai, who would not bow.

en: Although the seudah of Purim Katan is not obligatory, rejoicing with the Ribono shel Olam fulfils the Rema's closing words in Shulchan Aruch.
Milah is done at eight days, without da'as, and precisely so it binds the child to the hidden root of Avraham Avinu and of the Jewish people.
On Purim one rejoices with the hidden point in every Jew, the concealed love one does not even feel.
Milah, without da'as, and tefillin, which require da'as, are bound together, and Purim, with 'sasson' as milah and 'yekar' as tefillin, unites them.
A Jew's mesiras nefesh comes from the root above da'as, and the decree to bow to Haman was there to draw it out of Mordechai.

He asks why milah is not delayed until bar mitzvah and answers that without da'as the child is bound to the hidden root.

title.en: The hidden point, milah, tefillin and mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that on Purim one rejoices with the hidden love in every Jew, like an infant at his bris; he pairs milah, without da'as, with tefillin, which demand da'as, through the Gemara's reading of 'orah v'simchah v'sasson vikar'. Mesiras nefesh comes from this hidden root, as with Mordechai who would not bow to Haman, and he closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין "ואין נוהגין כן וכו' וטוב לב משתה תמיד" (סיום שו”ע או”ח רמ"א)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Rema's closing words on Purim Katan, why he tells us to eat a little more at a meal though the custom does not follow the Ran, and how 'vetov lev mishteh tamid' lets one satisfy the stringent view without breaking the minhag.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, where the Rema brings the Ran's view that Purim Katan requires feasting, notes that the custom follows Tosfos, yet says to eat a little more 'to satisfy the stringent', closing with 'vetov lev mishteh tamid'. Since the Rema guards every minhag, why add this? The Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham that one who experienced a miracle should make that day a yom tov, which the Chasam Sofer derives from the Gemara's kal vachomer about Hallel, and the Magen Avraham that a yahrzeit is kept in both Adars. Purim's own mishteh is a special din tied to wine, because the miracle came through wine. So even Tosfos agrees one should rejoice on Purim Katan; the dispute is only about wine. The Rema's answer is that Jews always say l'chaim. The Mashgiach closes with Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman.

en: The Mashgiach says the Rema guards every minhag, so his instruction to eat a little more on Purim Katan, against the custom he himself records, needs an explanation.
According to the Magen Avraham, anyone who experiences a miracle should make that day a yom tov, as with Purim Krakow, and the Chasam Sofer calls this a mitzvah learned by kal vachomer from Pesach.
The mishteh of Purim is not the general din of celebrating a miracle but a special halachah requiring wine, because the Purim miracle came about through wine.
Even Tosfos agrees one should rejoice on Purim Katan by the Magen Avraham's din; the difference is that only by the Ran's view must one drink wine.

The Rema's closing words 'vetov lev mishteh tamid' show how to satisfy the stringent view: Jews always say l'chaim at a gathering, so drinking a little wine does not look like going against the minhag.
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman whose family became Jews through the Purim miracle, had special reason for joy, which is why his son taught 'mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha'.

title.en: The last siman of Orach Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim on the 14th and 15th of Adar Rishon, the Mishnah that the two Adars differ only in Megillah and gifts to the poor, and the Rema's gloss ending with 'vetov lev mishteh tamid'. He says every word of the Rema is ruach hakodesh and deserves closer thought.

title.en: The Rema's strictness about minhag

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out the dispute between the Ran, who requires feasting on Purim Katan, and Tosfos, whom the custom follows. He shows the Rema's zeal for minhag with the example of shevarim-teruah blown in two breaths, and asks why the Rema then tells us to eat a little more at a meal.

title.en: A private Purim and a yahrzeit in Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham that a community or individual who experienced a miracle should make that day a yom tov, like Purim Krakow, and the Chasam Sofer who derives this mitzvah from the Gemara's kal vachomer about Hallel. He then brings the Magen Avraham that a yahrzeit is kept in both Adars, since only the Megillah is limited to the second Adar by the word 'hasheinis'.

title.en: Why Purim's feast needs wine

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Ran's view that Purim Katan requires a feast, and asks why Chanukah has no din of mishteh vesimcha despite the kal vachomer. He answers that the mishteh of Purim is a special din, a remembrance of a miracle that came through wine, so by the Ran one must drink wine on Purim Katan too.

title.en: Even Tosfos agrees to rejoice

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Tosfos does not require rejoicing on Purim Katan by the Magen Avraham's din, and answers that Tosfos too would agree to that. The difference is that a self-made yom tov like Purim Krakow can be celebrated in any way, even a parade, while Purim Gadol has halachos from Chazal that require wine.

title.en: Rereading the Rema: a l'chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach rereads the Rema phrase by phrase and points to the change of wording from 'mishteh vesimcha' to 'yarbeh ketzas biseudah'. He asks how a meal without wine satisfies the stringent view, and answers from 'vetov lev mishteh tamid': Jews always say l'chaim with a little wine, so one fulfills the Ran's view without visibly going against the minhag.

title.en: Wine or any strong drink?

summary.en: The Mashgiach wonders whether the Purim drinking must be wine or any intoxicating drink, since the custom is to drink bronfen. He notes that wine is named at Vashti's feast while Esther's feasts mention only 'mishteh', contrasts kiddush where wine is required, mentions Rabbi Avraham of Tshechanov drinking a revi'is of wine on Purim, and remarks that bronfen is a newer drink.

title.en: Haman's descendant and the joy of Adar

summary.en: Short of time, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that 'mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha' was said by Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas. From the Gemara that Haman's descendants taught Torah in Bnei Brak, he identifies Rav Shmuel bar Shilas as a descendant of Haman who would not have been a Jew without the Purim miracle, and so had special joy in Adar; he closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: The Theme of the Day - Proclaiming Hashem as King

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rosh Hashanah is at heart the coronation of Hashem as King, and that the judgment of the day follows from Hashem creating a new and better world each year, in which a person must earn a place by improving.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the principle that whatever happened in the Torah repeats itself every year, so on Rosh Hashanah Hashem re-creates the world, the ten days of teshuvah matching the ten utterances of creation. He notes that the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur brachos speak only of Malchus, Hashem's kingship, and hardly mention judgment. Citing his Rebbe, he explains that the judgment is a byproduct of the coronation: re-creating His world, Hashem decides who fits its purpose. Drawing on the Tanya, he adds that each year's world is higher than the last, so being as good as last year is not enough; one must improve. Shabbos Shuvah makes every Jew a partner in the new creation, and Yom Kippur, the tenth day, is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the calendar, when each Jew should reach the inner point of his heart that wants only Hashem's will.

en: Every event in the Torah repeats itself each year, so on Rosh Hashanah and in the ten days that follow Hashem creates the world anew.
The brachos of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are about Malchus, the coronation of Hashem, and do not speak of the day as a day of judgment.
The judgment is a byproduct of the coronation: as Hashem makes His new world, He decides who will serve its purpose and who would spoil it.
Each year's world is higher than the last, so being as good as last year is not enough; a person must improve to fit into the new year.
Through keeping Shabbos Shuvah properly a Jew becomes Hashem's partner in creating the new year.
Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim in time, and on it every Jew should reach the inner chamber of his heart that wants only to do Hashem's will.

title.en: Creation repeats every Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that events in the Torah are not commemorations but repeat every year, like the geulah of Nisan and Kabbalas HaTorah on Shavuos. So the creation of the world repeats each Rosh Hashanah, with each of the ten days matching one of the ten utterances, which is why a year is called shanah, a repetition.

title.en: Malchus, and why it is a day of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Shemoneh Esrei of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is entirely about Malchus, Hashem's coronation, and that the mention of judgment in Zichronos is not the core of the day. He brings his Rebbe's explanation: since Hashem re-creates the world, He decides who fits its purpose and who would spoil it, so the judgment is a byproduct of the coronation day, while the day itself is one of joy.

title.en: Each year a better world

summary.en: Adding to his Rebbe's words, the Mashgiach says Hashem does not duplicate last year's world but creates a better one, even if the streets and the shuls seem to show decline. He brings the sefarim that the world improves with each generation, and Rebbe Reb Bunim's teaching that although earlier souls were greater, the innermost point of the heart becomes better in every generation.

title.en: Last year's mark is not enough

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the Tanya that each Rosh Hashanah the light of the past year withdraws and a new, higher light comes down. From this he concludes that a person who is merely no worse than last year is failing the test, since he must be promoted into a better world, and he brings the piyut's call to improve one's deeds as the heavens themselves are improved.

title.en: Shabbos Shuvah: partner in the new creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, and especially on Shabbos Shuvah, Hashem takes each Jew as a partner in creating the new year, since keeping Shabbos is testimony to creation. He urges a Shabbos like never before, with a cheshbon hanefesh, care in its laws, Torah and davening, and joy, and brings the Shelah and the passuk in Tehillim that one should give Hashem pleasure and nachas.

title.en: Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim of the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur is the tenth day, parallel to the tenth utterance and the tenth level of holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, and that each Jew who does teshuvah enters it with the Kohen Gadol in his soul. Every Jew carries an inner chamber in his heart that wants only Hashem's will, as the Rambam explains, and on Yom Kippur he should dig to reach it. He closes noting the days left until Yom Kippur and asking to daven for Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: סעודת פורים קטן

oneLiner.en: On Purim Katan the Mashgiach explains, following the Chasam Sofer, that the joy of Purim stands on its own, and shows through the image of the Megillah as a kallah why that joy can join the joy of a chasan and kallah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer: rejoicing over a miracle, like the song sung over the redemption of Pesach, is itself an obligation, but the Torah gives no details, so the Sages set the seudah, matanos la'evyonim and mishloach manos. The joy itself, he says, is the deeper layer, and the Chasam Sofer holds that the seudah is not the only way to fulfill it. This, he explains, is the reason of the Yerushalmi that a Purim seudah falling on Shabbos is moved to Sunday: two joys are not mixed. That raises a question about joining a wedding's joy with Purim. The Mashgiach answers with the passuk that Hashem does not reject Israel even in exile, the mashal of a king who goes to his kallah even in a disgraceful place, and Rashi's teaching that the twenty-four books are like a kallah's adornments. Megillas Esther became a kallah, so its joy is a kallah's joy, and there is no contradiction. He closes with a brachah for Yerushalayim.

en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that the joy over the Purim miracle is an obligation in its own right, while the Sages only set its details: the seudah, gifts to the poor and mishloach manos.
The Mashgiach says this is the reason of the Yerushalmi that a Purim seudah falling on Shabbos is made on Sunday: two joys may not be mixed together.
Each of the twenty-four books is a kallah, and Megillas Esther, once it became one of them, became a kallah; the joy of the Megillah is the joy of a kallah.
The joy of Purim is a joy with the Jewish people in all their situations, even the lowest, and that is its connection to the joy of a kallah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the silver of the shekalim carries the power of love for Hashem, that Parshas Shekalim corresponds to the yud and the tip of the yud of Hashem's Name, the Jew's inner point that no sin and no Haman can reach, and he shows this through the haftarah of Yehoash.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe's accounting of the Mishkan's silver and the Gemara that Hashem preceded Haman's shekalim with ours. Everything in the world has a spiritual root: silver is the measure of love, gold of awe, and Hashem knows how many 'units' of love lie in a half-shekel. Adar is the month of Yosef and of blessing, which multiplies a hundredfold; this answers Tosafos' question how a hundred kikar of shekalim outweighed Haman's ten thousand. Adar's task is to complete Hashem's Name broken by Amalek, and Shekalim corresponds to the yud and its tip, the Kodesh HaKodashim. The haftarah's King Yehoash, saved in the Kodesh HaKodashim yet later the killer of Zechariah there, belongs to Parshas Shekalim, and his rescue shows that the innermost point of a Jew cannot be touched by sin. This point is revealed on Purim, which the Mashgiach calls greater than Yom Kippur.

en: Silver is the measure of love and gold the measure of awe; a half-shekel of silver holds a set measure of love for Hashem, and that, not the cold metal, is what Hashem asked the Jews to give.
Adar is the month of blessing and of Yosef, and blessing multiplies up to a hundredfold, which is why the hundred kikar the Jews gave became ten thousand and outweighed Haman's ten thousand kikar.
Amalek broke Hashem's Name, and the work of Adar, through the four parshiyos and the four mitzvos of Purim, is to make the Name whole again.
Parshas Shekalim corresponds to the yud of Hashem's Name and to its tip, the Kodesh HaKodashim, the source from which everything comes.
Every Jew has an inner point, his own Kodesh HaKodashim, that no sin can blemish and no mitzvah can add to, and Purim reveals it.
Yehoash's soul is rooted in Parshas Shekalim, and the Kodesh HaKodashim saved him even though he would later defile it, to show that nothing can blemish that place.
