title.en: Moshe's accounting of the silver; Rosh Chodesh Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Moshe gives an exact accounting only for the silver of the Mishkan, and that the words 'a kikar for each socket' seem superfluous. He then turns to Rosh Chodesh Adar and the Gemara that Hashem preceded Haman's shekalim with the Jews' shekalim, and promises an approach that answers the commentators' questions.

title.en: The world as text, the Torah as commentary

summary.en: Each of the Mishkan's materials had its own segulah. The Mashgiach brings the Kotzker's saying that the world is Hashem's composition and the Torah its commentary, and explains that an ehrlicher Yid sees white as chesed and love, red as awe, and that love and awe are the most precious things in the world.

title.en: Silver as love, gold as awe, units of love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that kesef is love, from 'nichsof', and gold is awe, and that the half-shekel and the five sela'im of pidyon haben hold a measure of love set at creation, like units in a medicine. That measure can be increased by blessing, as with the generous man's bread, or lost, as with the miser's.

title.en: Adar, the month of Yosef and blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar is the month of blessing and of Yosef, whose blessing is increase; one month becomes two. He brings the Maharal on the letters of 'barech' and Yitzchak's hundredfold harvest, then raises Tosafos' difficult question about Haman's ten thousand kikar.

title.en: A hundredfold blessing answers Tosafos

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the shekalim, given in the month of blessing, were blessed a hundredfold, so the hundred kikar became ten thousand, matching Haman's gift; Haman sought the power of the number one hundred but the Jews preceded him. This also explains the 'kikar for each socket' of the opening question.

title.en: Completing Hashem's Name; the yud and its tip

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek broke Hashem's Name and that Adar's task is to make it whole, including answering 'yehei shmei rabba' with kavanah. The four parshiyos correspond to the four letters, and the yud with its tip is the beginning of everything; the four letters also correspond to the four elements.

title.en: Shekalim as the yud of fire; the haftarah

summary.en: Parshas Shekalim is the first parshah and corresponds to the yud and the element of fire, which explains why Moshe was shown a coin of fire. The Mashgiach then explains that a haftarah draws down and explains its parshah, and that the haftarah of Shekalim tells of Yehoash, who restored the giving of shekalim.

title.en: The story of Yehoash

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Yehoash was saved as a baby from Atalyah and hidden by Yehoyada in the Kodesh HaKodashim, became king and did right while Yehoyada lived, then let his servants treat him as a god and killed Zechariah ben Yehoyada in the Mikdash on Yom Kippur. He brings Yirmiyahu's lament and the lesson never to be sure of oneself.

title.en: Why Yehoash, and why was he saved?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the light of Parshas Shekalim, the tip of the yud and the Kodesh HaKodashim, is drawn down through Yehoash, who blemished the Kodesh HaKodashim, and why that very place saved him. He answers in part that a later merit can work retroactively, as with Avraham at Dan, since the kingdom of Beis David leading to Moshiach had to survive.

title.en: Purim and the point that cannot be erased

summary.en: Purim comes from the root of Jewish souls, the point in every Jew that cannot become wicked; the Chiddushei HaRim calls it the point of Avraham. Amalek attacked the stragglers, and Hashem's war against Amalek is over that point; therefore on Purim Jews rejoice simply in being Jews.

title.en: Purim, Yom Kippur and Haman's beam

summary.en: The Kodesh HaKodashim is the source of Yom Kippur's atonement and corresponds to the Kodesh HaKodashim in every Jew; Purim reveals it even more than Yom Kippur. Haman took a beam from the Kodesh HaKodashim for the gallows, and it took revenge on him; his slander 'yeshno am echad' could reach the later letters of the Name but not the yud and its tip.

title.en: Yehoash's letter is in Parshas Shekalim

summary.en: Every Jew has a letter in the Sefer Torah, which is why each is drawn to a particular mitzvah. Yehoash's letter is in Parshas Shekalim, his one good deed; so his rescue in the Kodesh HaKodashim teaches that Shekalim comes from a place no sin can blemish, and his name holds the letters of the Name with 'esh'. Adar, especially in a leap year, reveals the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.

title.en: The joy and greatness of Purim

summary.en: On Purim a Jew rejoices in being a Jew, since Purim reaches where mitzvos cannot. The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that the Torah and Megillas Esther will remain in the days of Moshiach and the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's light is greater than the Torah's, and says Purim must be prepared for with teshuvah and good deeds; its four mitzvos complete the Name.

catalogTitle: השקלים ששכח משה הציל את ישראל מהמן (התעוררות לאדר - פורים)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the extra half-shekels Moshe forgot came from the 'forgotten' Jews outside the camp, and that Hashem never forgets them; this is why Haman's shekalim failed and why Adar, the forgotten month, became a time of salvation and tefillah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that Moshe accounted for the silver of the half-shekels but forgot what he made from the extra 1,775 shekels, until he was reminded that they became the hooks of the pillars. He links this to Haman's ten thousand talents, which Tosafos matches to the shekalim of 600,000 Jews only, and asks why Haman ignored the 3,550 others. The answer runs through the stragglers of Shevet Dan, idol-worshippers pushed outside the camp, whom Amalek attacked; Parshas Zachor teaches that Hashem still loves them. These 'forgotten' Jews correspond to the last verses of the Torah, to the halachos forgotten when Moshe died, and to Adar, the forgotten thirteenth month. Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded Moshe, and 'the poor will not be forgotten forever.' The Mashgiach ends with the Chasam Sofer on Achashverosh's feast, the power of tefillah in Adar, the Yaaros Devash's long davening, and preparing for Purim's great light.

en: The extra 1,775 shekels from the 3,550 Jews beyond the 600,000 became the hooks (vavim) of the courtyard pillars, and Moshe forgot this until he was reminded.
Amalek attacked the stragglers of Shevet Dan, who had been pushed outside the camp for idol worship, thinking such Jews were no longer bound to Hashem.
Every Jew carries a hidden love and faith from Avraham Avinu that is never extinguished, so Hashem never gives up on any Jew.
Adar is the 'forgotten' month, matching the forgotten Jews outside the camp, yet Hashem remembered it and turned it into a month of joy.
Purim came through tefillah and fasting, so Taanis Esther is part of Purim, and Adar is an especially favorable time for tefillah.
Purim brings down a great light, and one must prepare for it beforehand with Torah and tefillah, just as one prepares all week for Shabbos.

candidateTopics: the half-shekel and the hooks of the pillars
Rabbi Akiva and the crowns of the letters

title.en: Adar's favor and the shekels Moshe forgot

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling these days of Adar a time of favor for tefillah, hinted in Mordechai 'ben Kish', who knocked on the gates of mercy. He brings the Midrash on Parshas Shekalim and the Midrash that Moshe forgot what he made from the extra 1,775 shekels until a voice reminded him of the hooks of the pillars, and asks how Moshe, who never forgot Torah, could forget.

title.en: Haman's ten thousand talents

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Haman offered ten thousand talents of silver and Hashem answered that Israel's shekalim came first, and Tosafos' calculation that this equals the half-shekels of the 600,000. He asks why Haman paid nothing against the shekalim of the extra 3,550 Jews.

title.en: Shevet Dan and the stragglers outside the camp

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shevet Dan marched last in the camp and that some of them carried Micha's idol through the sea, so the clouds expelled them outside the camp. Amalek could only attack these stragglers, as the Targum explains 'all the weak ones behind you'.

title.en: Why Zachor must be read from a Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Parshas Zachor, of all Torah readings, must be heard from a Sefer Torah. He explains the rule that the written Torah may not be said by heart: only in the scroll does one see full and missing spellings, extra letters and crowns that Chazal and Rabbi Akiva expounded, and only a complete scroll shows which parsha stands beside which.

title.en: The hidden love in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem is so angry at Amalek for attacking idol-worshippers, and answers that every child of Avraham keeps a hidden faith and love that waits for a time of favor, like a contagious patient whom only the great doctor can heal. Therefore Parshas Zachor, read from the scroll so every Jew understands it, strengthens every Jew in whatever state he is that Hashem has not given up on him.

title.en: The hooks outside the courtyard and the letters of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even the Jews outside the camp gave the half-shekel, and their silver became the hooks that joined the curtains to the pillars and hung partly outside the holy courtyard. He adds that every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah, and brings the Yismach Moshe that every Jew also corresponds to one Shabbos of history, so each Shabbos may be 'his'.

title.en: The Torah's last verses and the forgotten month

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute over who wrote the last eight verses of the Torah and suggests that the Jews corresponding to them are the 'forgotten' ones outside the camp, matching the three thousand halachos forgotten when Moshe died. He then ties the twelve tribes to the twelve months: Dan to Adar, and those expelled from the camp to Adar Sheni, which according to the Bnei Yissaschar has no permutation of Hashem's name.

title.en: Haman's lottery lands on Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Targum that Haman's lottery passed over every day and month because each had a merit for Israel, until it fell on Adar. He asks why Moshe's birth on the seventh of Adar was no merit, and answers that Adar is a month of forgetting, when the merit was forgotten; yet Hashem says through Yeshayahu that He will not forget.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva reminds Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the opening question: Moshe forgot the extra shekels because they came from souls of forgetting, and the soul of Rabbi Akiva, who could expound even the crowns of the letters, reminded him that they were the hooks. He links Rabbi Akiva to 'ikvesa d'Meshicha' and to our generation, in which most Jews are like the stragglers, and says Amalek erred in thinking a sinning Jew is cut off from Hashem.

title.en: Haman's mistake and Adar turned around

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman made Amalek's mistake: he paid only for the 600,000 and ignored the 3,550 as forgotten idol-worshippers, but Hashem does not forget even the lowest Jew. He brings that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, with Adar belonging to Esav, and Mordechai seized it, turning it into a month remembered with joy and a time of teshuvah.

title.en: A miracle in the midst of the feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that the decree came because the Jews enjoyed Achashverosh's feast, which celebrated his reckoning that the seventy years had passed and the Beis Hamikdash would not be rebuilt. Yet in the midst of that sin Hashem began the miracle with Vashti's death, which shows how much Hashem loves the Jews, and on Purim they accepted the Torah out of love.

title.en: Adar, a month of tefillah, and Taanis Esther

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that even those who crossed the sea with Micha's idol gave a half-shekel, which outweighs Haman's silver, and calls Adar a month of remembering and turning over. He explains that Purim came through tefillah, answers how one may fast on Taanis Esther the day before a yom tov, and calls on every serious bochur to gather merits of Torah and tefillah in this time of trouble.

title.en: The Megillah is full of tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that 'leha'avir gilulim min ha'aretz' spells Megillah, compares the state of the Jews then, who needed Nechemiah to separate them from intermarriage, to today, and urges davening for all Jews. He cites the Gemara that tefillah stands at the height of the world yet people treat it lightly, and shows from the Targum that Mordechai and Esther davened throughout the Megillah.

title.en: The Yaaros Devash's long davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the Yaaros Devash a letter of Rabbi Yonasan Eibeschutz to the Rav of Königsberg explaining why he davens long despite his teaching and the mockery of others: his portion from all his toil is standing before the One Who hears tefillah. The Mashgiach concludes that one must strike while the iron is hot, as Mordechai knocked on the gates of mercy, with Torah and good davening.

title.en: Preparing for the light of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the great light that comes down on Purim, greater even than Shabbos according to sefarim and the Chasam Sofer, and compares it to Shabbos, whose fire must be kindled all week. He says Purim's joy differs from Yom Kippur, calls for preparing now with Torah and tefillah, and closes on the hope that this generation can bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: ר”ה שחל בשבת - Developing a Relationship with our Advocate

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is silent, Shabbos itself becomes the advocate of the Jewish people, so before the Day of Judgment one must make peace with Shabbos and learn to keep it properly.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a parable, adapted from a sefer's Rosh Hashanah drasha for a year when Rosh Hashanah fell on Shabbos: a king's faithful servant dies, and his son is sent to mine gems for the king but neglects his task. Each year the finance minister pleads for him, but one year the minister is absent and the princess, whom the son had abused, takes his place; a wise man tells him to beg her forgiveness, and she pleads his case. The Mashgiach explains: the king is Hashem, the gems are Torah and mitzvos, the regular advocate is the shofar, and when Rosh Hashanah is on Shabbos, Shabbos, the king's daughter and our cousin, pleads instead. Since we have wronged Shabbos, we must make up with her: learn hilchos Shabbos, refine Shabbos speech, and fill Shabbos with kedushah and joy, illustrated by two stories of tzaddikim. He closes urging a new kabbalah in the area of Shabbos for this year.

en: In an ordinary year the shofar is the advocate that pleads for Klal Yisrael on Rosh Hashanah, carrying their teshuvah before Hashem.

When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is not blown, Shabbos itself takes over as the advocate, and since Shabbos is the King's daughter and bound up with the Jewish soul, an even better year can be expected.
Because Jews have wronged Shabbos through chillul Shabbos, they must make peace with Shabbos through teshuvah before Rosh Hashanah, so that she pleads for them rather than against them.
One cannot keep Shabbos properly without knowing hilchos Shabbos, which are numerous and complex, so the Mashgiach calls for learning them until one masters them.

Keeping Shabbos means more than avoiding its prohibitions: it is a day of rest and kedushah, with refined speech and a way of spending it that gives pleasure to Shabbos, which then gives pleasure back.
For a Jew who keeps it properly, Shabbos is the most joyous day of the week, a pleasure no worldly delight can match.

title.en: Parable of the king, the gems and the princess

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable of a faithful servant's son sent to mine gems for the king, who neglects his work and is saved each year by the finance minister, until one year the princess he had abused must judge him and a wise man tells him to beg her forgiveness. He says he adapted it from a sefer's drasha for a Rosh Hashanah that fell on Shabbos.

title.en: The nimshal: the shofar as our advocate

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the parable: the king is Hashem, the beloved servant is the Avos, the gems are Torah and mitzvos the Jews must produce in this world, and the friendly minister is the shofar, whose every sound is a plea for forgiveness accompanied by the teshuvah of the Jewish heart.

title.en: When Rosh Hashanah is Shabbos, Shabbos pleads

summary.en: When Rosh Hashanah is on Shabbos and the shofar is not blown, Shabbos, the King's daughter and the Jew's cousin through the neshamah yeseirah, takes over the case; the Mashgiach brings the seforim's reading of 'Tiku bachodesh shofar' whose initials spell Shabbos. But since Jews have abused Shabbos, the Torah, the wise man of the court, tells them to do teshuvah, beg Shabbos's forgiveness and promise to keep her.

title.en: Making peace with Shabbos: learning its halachos

summary.en: Since Shabbos rather than the shofar will plead this Rosh Hashanah, the Mashgiach says one must first be on good terms with Shabbos. He challenges the assumption that one keeps Shabbos already: without knowing the many complex halachos, such as the thirty-nine melachos, borer and muktzeh, one surely stumbles, so one should resolve to learn hilchos Shabbos thoroughly.

title.en: Beyond the prohibitions: holy speech and rest

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that avoiding issurim is not enough: Shabbos is a day of rest and kedushah. Since Hashem created the world in six days through speech, one rests on Shabbos by refining one's speech; Shabbos is not for sleeping and reading the newspaper but for kedushah and tefillah, and when a Jew gives Shabbos pleasure, Shabbos reciprocates.

title.en: The poritz's summer sled and Nishmas

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a poritz who spread sugar on a meadow to go sled riding in August; a chassid told his Rebbe how the poritz enjoys the world, and the Rebbe answered that it could not compare to his pleasure saying Nishmas on Shabbos morning. He contrasts people who complain Shabbos is boring with a Jew who keeps Shabbos and is repaid with a pleasure beyond anything worldly.

title.en: Reb Moshe Leib Sassover at the poritz's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Reb Moshe Leib Sassover, who went to the paritzim to redeem Jews imprisoned for unpaid rent; at a poritz's feast on a fast day, the aroma of a costly dish endangered him, and he saved himself by recalling his pleasure saying Nishmas on Shabbos. The Mashgiach concludes that Shabbos is the most joyous day, but only for one who keeps it as it should be kept.

title.en: A new kabbalah for Shabbos this year

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges keeping Shabbos as the day of Hashem's joy in His creation, and brings from seforim that on Rosh Hashanah each person should take on a new hanhagah; he suggests it be in the area of Shabbos, so that one can say 'Retzei vimnuchaseinu' to Hashem. He notes that this year Shabbos reigns, with Rosh Hashanah, Sukkos and two Shabbosos of Chanukah, and closes with a brachah for the eternal Shabbos.

catalogTitle: אם אתם תמחו עמלק מלבכם' אני אמחה אותו מעולם (התעוררות לפורים)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek's true root is the yetzer hara in the Jewish heart, which attacks both kedushas habris and emunah, and that Purim, the day of milah and tefillin, is the time to erase it with an emunah above the intellect.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah of erasing Amalek and asks how it can be fulfilled when nobody knows who Amalek is. Following the Alshich, he explains that every nation has a heavenly prince, but Amalek's prince is the yetzer hara itself, living in Jewish hearts; only the Jews can defeat it through teshuvah, and then physical Amalek falls on its own. Amalek attacks both kedushas habris and emunah, which are one, since emunah is Avraham's inheritance through the bris. Purim, a weekday Yom Tov of hidden miracles, is the time of clear emunah. Through the Gemara's teaching that sasson is milah and yikar is tefillin, he explains tefillin as emunah above the intellect, black in galus. After a hesped for a tzaddik who passed away that week, he calls our era the low point of time and Purim the preparation for the final Shabbos.

en: Amalek's heavenly prince is the yetzer hara in the Jewish heart, so the war against Amalek must be fought by the Jews themselves, with yiras Shamayim and teshuvah.
When the Jews erase Amalek from their hearts, Hashem erases the physical Amalek, which answers how the mitzvah can be fulfilled without knowing who Amalek is.
Amalek attacks kedushas habris and emunah, and the two are one, since emunah is Avraham Avinu's inheritance that comes through the bris.
Purim, a weekday Yom Tov whose miracles are hidden, is the month and day for strengthening clear emunah.
Tefillin, the 'yikar' of Purim, stand for emunah above the intellect, black because in galus there is no grasp, and this emunah in darkness is the glory of Klal Yisrael.
Our generation lives in the 'ervas hazman', the lowest point of time, and Purim gives the strength to hold on to emunah until the Shabbos of Moshiach.

candidateTopics: tefillin as emunah above the intellect

title.en: A mitzvah no one seems able to fulfill

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas Zachor and asks why the Torah gave the mitzvah of erasing Amalek, when Shaul did not fulfill it and since Sancheiriv mixed up the nations nobody knows who Amalek is. He reviews the pesukim about Amalek: how he cooled the Jews on the way, his attack on milah, and the war against him in every generation.

title.en: The Alshich: Amalek's prince is the yetzer hara

summary.en: Bringing the Alshich, the Mashgiach explains that every nation falls when Hashem topples its heavenly prince, but Amalek's prince is the yetzer hara inside Jewish hearts, which Hashem leaves to the Jews because of free choice. When they erase it through teshuvah, physical Amalek falls, which answers his opening question and the two pesukim of 'I will erase' and 'you shall erase'.

title.en: Amalek: blemish of the bris and doubt in emunah

summary.en: From the pesukim the Mashgiach shows that Amalek concentrates on two things, impure thoughts and attacking milah, and doubt in emunah, as Amalek equals safek in gematria. He explains that both are one, since the clear emunah of Jews is Avraham Avinu's inheritance through the bris, and guarding the bris keeps that emunah clear.

title.en: Purim: emunah in hiddenness, like Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar is the month for strengthening emunah: the Megillah has no open miracles and no Name of Hashem, yet one makes a brachah on its miracles, an emunah greater than that of Yetzias Mitzrayim. Purim was deliberately kept a weekday Yom Tov, and Yom Kippur, the day Avraham had his bris, is only 'like Purim'; he then brings the Gemara's 'orah, simchah, sasson and yikar'.

title.en: Why milah and tefillin, and where kefirah comes from

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the joy of Purim is milah and its glory is tefillin, and why intelligent people deny Hashem when the world shows Him so clearly. From Chazal's 'acharei levavchem, this is minus' he explains that heresy comes from the heart: a person who wants to justify a weakness or a desire invents a world-view that permits it, and so a blemish of the bris leads to kefirah.

title.en: Tefillin as the keser above the body

summary.en: Through Pesach Eliyahu the Mashgiach explains that the ten maamaros correspond to parts of the body, but keser is the tefillin, worn on the body yet not part of it, because Elokus is beyond even the mind and is reached only through emunah and kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim. Black tefillin and covered eyes at Shema express this; on Shabbos the clarity shines in and Shabbos itself is the tefillin, and Purim joins milah with tefillin.

title.en: Yikar in Targum: the glory of emunah in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why 'yikar' is an Aramaic, Targum word, and explains that Targum stands for galus and darkness, as the Chasam Sofer says about shnayim mikra v'echad targum. The tefillin of Purim are black Targum-tefillin, and the glory of Jews who believe and say Shema in the darkness of galus is a nachas ruach to Hashem greater than in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, as Hashem's own tefillin praise Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The heretic's demand for proof and the orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the heretic who refuses to accept anything his mind cannot grasp, and says the true reason is that he is not careful with milah. From the Ibn Ezra and Rambam on the orlah, an extra part on the body that must be removed, he answers that just as the body has something not belonging to it, it can carry something above it; this is the bond between sasson and yikar, and on Purim one surrenders one's daas to Hashem.

title.en: Hesped: a tzaddik of yesod

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of a tzaddik who passed away that week, the Gerer Rebbe, whose avodah was kedushah beyond the letter of the law, and tells how as a ten-year-old he leapt from a window rather than be alone with a disguised woman. Against those who mock such care as excessive, he brings Rashi that Avraham Avinu did not know how Sarah looked, because as the root of milah he had to pass on that guarding to his children.

title.en: The tzaddik's life left to the living

summary.en: The Mashgiach says earlier tzaddikim felt the darkness when a great tzaddik passed away, while today we do not. He brings the letter in Tanya on the passing of Rabbi Mendel of Vitebsk, that a tzaddik 'leaves life to all the living', and the Midrash that Yosef died but his Elokus remained, and connects it to Zayin Adar, when Moshe both died and was born.

title.en: Mitzrayim of time: the era before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham's episode with Sarah happened precisely in Mitzrayim, and explains that Mitzrayim is the 'ervas ha'aretz' where Amalek's klipah is strongest. Since place, time and soul parallel each other, there is also an 'ervas hazman', the era before Moshiach of heresy and immorality, in which we live; the last pasuk of Shema and Purim, the last month of the year, give strength for it, and the Megillah is spread out to spread emunah.

title.en: Purim as tefillin and preparation for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Purim is the day of black tefillin, emunah above daas in the drunkenness of galus, until the Shabbos of Moshiach when the grasp will be white. Like the sixth day that prepares for Shabbos, Purim prepares for it, and on Shabbos the Kedushah of Keser replaces tefillin; Parshas Zachor begins the preparation with teshuvah and not forgetting Hashem.

catalogTitle: ביאור הפטורה - מלכות שאול וטעם שהפסיד אותו (התעוררות לפורים)

oneLiner.en: Through the haftarah of Parshas Zachor, the Mashgiach explains that Shaul held a true, hereditary kingship and a chance to be Moshiach on the eve of Pesach, and lost it through one critical failing: he did not subordinate his own halachic reasoning to Shmuel, the elder of the generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Shaul lost his kingship over one sin while David kept his despite two, and with the Midrash that Shaul's kingship was only 'borrowed'. He then builds the idea of hereditary office: one who holds authority over Jews cannot be removed and his son inherits it, because all authority is appointed by Heaven and true kingship mirrors Hashem's eternal kingship. Eisav has no 'king son of king', since its rule is service, not kingship, borrowed from Israel. Shaul's reign came when Edom's eight kings had ended, and before David's promise Moshiach could come from any tribe, so Shaul's war on Amalek on the eve of Pesach could have brought the redemption. Shaul reasoned halachically to spare Amalek's women and animals, but failed by not deferring to Shmuel. The Mashgiach contrasts Esther, who obeyed Mordechai even as queen, and closes on Purim: the reversal of Amalek, a festival for broken Jews, and this year's three-day Purim in Jerusalem.

en: The Mashgiach asks why Shaul lost his kingship over a single sin while David, who stumbled twice, kept his, especially since the Midrash says Shaul's kingship was only borrowed from the start.

Any office of authority among Jews, from king and kohen gadol down to chazan and melamed, passes to a fitting son, because every such authority is appointed by Heaven and true kingship reflects Hashem's eternal kingship.
Eisav has no 'king son of king' because its rulers are servants of the people rather than kings, and whatever rule it has is borrowed from Israel until Israel takes it back.
Shaul's war against Amalek fell on the eve of Pesach, the time destined for the destruction of Amalek, so Shaul could have become Moshiach had he fulfilled the command that very day.

Shaul's failing was not disobedience to prophecy but a refusal to subordinate his own halachic reasoning to Shmuel, the elder of the generation; since Amalek is the opposite of self-nullification, the war against it demands such subordination.
Purim, whose festive meal is held on a weekday, is the time of reversal when what Eisav took is returned to holiness, and it was made especially for Jews who feel broken and far.

candidateTopics: war against Amalek on erev Pesach
deference to the elder of the generation

title.en: Shaul lost his kingdom over one sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the haftarah of Parshas Zachor, where Shmuel sends Shaul to war against Amalek, and notes that had Shaul obeyed fully, Haman would never have been born. He then asks, from the Gemara in Yoma, why Shaul lost his kingship over one sin while David, who stumbled twice, did not.

title.en: Yaakov's blessing and a borrowed kingship

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the blessing to Yaakov after his struggle with Eisav's angel, that kings would come from him, which Rashi explains as Shaul and Ish-Boshes, and asks what blessing lies in Ish-Boshes's brief, tragic reign. He adds the Midrash that Shaul was so named because the kingship was only borrowed, and asks what Shaul's sin then cost him.

title.en: Authority over Jews passes to the son

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out the halacha that one appointed to an office among Jews, a chazan, rav, gabbai or melamed, cannot be dismissed and a fitting son inherits it, as the Rambam rules for a king and a kohen gadol. He gives the reason that every such office is appointed by Heaven, and then asks how the Rema allows a condition that the appointment is only temporary.

title.en: Kingship belongs to Hashem alone

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Avodah Zarah on Ovadiah's prophecy that Eisav has no 'king son of king', and distinguishes kingship from mere service. He explains that kingship belongs only to Hashem, which is why Moshe honored Pharaoh and Eliyahu honored Achav, and that a human king is a vessel for Hashem's kingship, which is eternal and therefore passes from father to son.

title.en: Why Eisav has no king son of king

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Eisav's rulers are servants of the people, not kings, because Eisav has no real existence or inheritance of its own and lives only on what it takes from Yaakov, as Rashi says on 'one nation shall prevail over the other'. From this he answers the Rema: a chazan appointed on a temporary condition is a servant, not a holder of kingship, so the condition does not contradict the Torah.

title.en: The kings of Edom and Shaul's name

summary.en: From the end of Parshas Vayishlach the Mashgiach shows that Edom had kings only before Israel had a king, and that none of its eight kings was the son of a king. He wonders why Kish named his son Shaul, a name found among Edom's kings, and compares the Chasam Sofer's comment on Korach's name.

title.en: Shaul's chance to be Moshiach on erev Pesach

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer on 'the scepter shall not depart from Yehudah', the Mashgiach explains that before David received the promise Moshiach could come from any tribe, so Shaul, reigning once Edom's kings had ended, could himself have been Moshiach. He brings that the war against Amalek is destined for the eve of Pesach, and shows from the Targum that Shaul counted the people with Pesach lambs, so his war fell on that very day.

title.en: Why Shaul did not obey the navi

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a king could disobey a navi, and brings the Gemara that Shaul reasoned by kal vachomer from the eglah arufah not to kill Amalek's women, children and animals. He explains that Shmuel told him two things, a prophecy that now was the appointed time and a halacha from his own understanding, and Shaul disputed only the halacha, yet his whole kingship and the chance for redemption hung on it.

title.en: Bowing to the elder of the generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek is the opposite of self-nullification, and tells how the Chasam Sofer explained to his son that in each generation one person is the decisor of Klal Yisrael. Shmuel was that elder in his day, and Shaul's error was not yielding to him; one mistake, but a critical one, whereas David's lapses did not touch his standing.

title.en: A flaw in outlook, Esther, and Ish-Boshes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David's faults came from the yetzer hara while his emunah stayed whole, but Shaul's flaw was in his outlook, and contrasts Esther, who kept obeying Mordechai even as queen. He describes the golden future Shaul lost by one day, as Agag's seed lived on that Pesach night, and answers why Ish-Boshes was a blessing: he showed that Shaul's kingship was a true, hereditary one.

title.en: Purim reverses Amalek's hold

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that on Purim the Jews took over Haman's house and wealth, and explains Purim as the reversal in which what Eisav took is returned to holiness: the Purim meal is held on a weekday to elevate kelipas nogah, which only a Jew can do. He brings the Chasam Sofer that 'mishteh vesimchah' turns the death of Moshe into the life of Moshe, and says Purim was made for Jews who feel broken.

title.en: Purim as revival and love

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Purim as a powerful remedy that revives Jews in whom the spark of Moshe seemed dead, a new light greater even than at Matan Torah because then the Torah was accepted out of love. He brings that on Purim a great light from above is revealed that reaches even the farthest Jew, like a father who reaches his most soiled child.

title.en: Shushan, Jerusalem and the three-day Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Megillah's count of the Jews in Shushan against the rest, explains that Shushan Purim today belongs to Jerusalem, whose Jews are the heart of the world, and notes that this year Purim in Jerusalem lasts three days. He calls Purim greater even than Yom Kippur, too bright to bear without drink, and closes by urging not to waste the opportunity, as preparation thirty days before Pesach.

catalogTitle: בשבת זו יכולים לעקור חיות של עמלק. פורים - גדלות היום והדרכה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that through the reading of Parshas Zachor one can uproot the inner life-force of Amalek, and describes the greatness of Purim and how to prepare for it and conduct it with holiness and seriousness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas Zachor, the one Torah reading that is a mitzvah from the Torah. Everything has a hidden life-force, and so does Amalek, whose soul cools a Jew's emunah and makes people sin. One cannot fight Amalek with weapons, and even Yehoshua only weakened him; his full erasure waits for Moshiach. But through hearing Parshas Zachor one can weaken the Amalek, the yetzer hara, within oneself. He urges teshuvah as preparation, a proper Friday night, saying Hodu with fire, and joining the zemiros at the tisch. He then turns to Purim: the three days before it are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, Purim is compared to Yom Kippur, and on it one can be reconciled with Hashem and ask for anything. Its holiness is so great that the Megillah is opened completely, and it reaches above the Name Havaya, hidden in its verses. He warns firmly against drinking and smoking on Purim, and closes with Esther as the moon of Adar and a call to come to davening on time.

en: Everything has a hidden life-force, and Amalek's inner life-force is what cools the emunah of Jews and makes them sin.
Amalek cannot be wiped out entirely before Moshiach, but through the reading of Parshas Zachor one can weaken the Amalek, the yetzer hara, that every person carries within himself.
The Mashgiach calls for preparing for Shabbos Zachor with teshuvah, saying Hodu with fire, and coming to the Friday night tisch to sing zemiros with joy.
Purim is compared to Yom Kippur; on it one can be reconciled with Hashem and ask for anything, and even the lowest Jew is dear.
Purim's holiness spreads over everything, which is why the whole Megillah is opened, and it comes from a level above the Name Havaya, hidden in the verses of the Megillah.
The Mashgiach warns that Purim must be spent with seriousness, without getting drunk and without smoking, since many became addicted through Purim.

title.en: Uprooting Amalek's life-force through Parshas Zachor

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every thing has a hidden life-force, and so does Amalek, which cools emunah and makes people sin. Amalek cannot be fought with weapons and will be fully erased only by Moshiach, as even Yehoshua only weakened him, but by hearing Parshas Zachor each person can weaken the Amalek within himself.

title.en: Preparing for Shabbos: Hodu and the Friday night tisch

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for teshuvah before Parshas Zachor and a proper Friday night: saying Hodu with fire rather than standing at the bulletin board, since through it one binds oneself to the Ba'al Shem Tov and Dovid HaMelech. He tells of a Rebbe who told a bochur that coming to the tisch to sing zemiros with joy is more important than saying all of Tehillim before davening.

title.en: Purim like Yom Kippur: a day of reconciliation and giving

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Warker Rebbe that the three days before Purim are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos, and that Purim is compared to Yom Kippur. On Purim one can be reconciled with Hashem, who shows His love to the lowest Jew, and just as one gives to whoever stretches out a hand, Hashem gives to whoever asks.

title.en: The crown-holiness of Purim and the open Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the holiness of Keser that appears on Shabbos and Yom Kippur rests on Purim the whole day, so Purim is no day for cigars and jokes but for joy with trembling. Holy things are usually covered, like the shofar, the challos and the Sefer Torah, but the whole Megillah is opened because Purim's holiness spreads over the whole world.

title.en: Above the Name Havaya: Hashem hidden in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Purim, like Yom Kippur, comes from a level higher than the Name Havaya, which is why no Name appears in the Megillah except hidden in the first and last letters of words. He shows it in 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' and in 'zeh einenu shoveh li', and explains that on Purim Hashem asks Klal Yisroel what they wish for.

title.en: A warning against drinking and smoking on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against getting drunk on Purim: though the Satmar Rav drank much, he himself said the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples did not drink on Purim, and ordinary people are better off not drinking. He describes people who became alcoholics and smokers through Purim, explains that the habit cannot then be stopped, and allows only a cup of wine.

title.en: Esther the moon of Adar; come on time to davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects Kiddush Levanah of Adar with Esther, whom the Gemara links to the moon, mentions the hilula of the Kaliver Rebbe and his holy Hungarian niggunim, and closes by urging everyone to come on time to davening on Shabbos Zachor and Purim, with fire and kavanah.

catalogTitle: The Multiplied קדושה and Cleansing Power of יו”כ when it Coincides with שבת

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Yom Kippur which falls on Shabbos carries a compounded kedushah and a cleansing power beyond that of an ordinary Yom Kippur, and calls for a Shabbos kept in true kedushah.

abstract.en: After explaining why he speaks in English, the Mashgiach cites Chazal's reading of 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the ten days of teshuvah, when the Shechinah comes down to us. The Ba'alei Mussar explain it through the Gemara in Yoma about the butcher who ignored Rav standing at his door: the opportunity is a blessing, but a warning to whoever lets it pass. On Yom Kippur the kedushah comes to every Jew, and the Sefer Torah is carried around for everyone to ask its forgiveness. A Yom Kippur on Shabbos is a double Shabbos; the Arvei Nachal's mashal shows Shabbos and Torah as the king's children who plead for Klal Yisrael. The Mashgiach then urges a Shabbos of real kedushah, without newspapers or idle talk. He concludes, citing the Taz, that Shabbos together with Yom Kippur atones even for sins Yom Kippur alone cannot, and that the world's turmoil is a time to hope for Moshiach.

en: Chazal read 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the ten days of teshuvah, when Hashem lowers Himself and makes Himself available to us.
Hashem's availability is a blessing, but whoever ignores it, like the butcher who ignored Rav, is punished all the more.
When Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos, each strengthens the other and the kedushah of the day is compounded.
Keeping the prohibitions of Shabbos is not enough; Shabbos must be made holy with Torah, tefillah and song, not newspapers or idle talk.
Shabbos together with Yom Kippur atones even for sins that Yom Kippur alone leaves a mark on.

title.en: Seek Hashem when He is found

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why he speaks in English, then brings Chazal's reading of 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the time the Shechinah descends to us. The Ba'alei Mussar explain it with the Gemara in Yoma about Rav, who went to a butcher who had not asked his forgiveness, and the butcher who ignored him and died.

title.en: An opportunity and a warning

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the lesson: in the ten days the Shechinah comes down to inspire teshuvah, but woe to one who ignores it. On Yom Kippur night every Jew feels the kedushah, and the Sefer Torah is carried to everyone to kiss it and ask its forgiveness.

title.en: A double Shabbos and the Arvei Nachal's mashal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that this Yom Kippur coincides with Shabbos, a 'double Shabbos' that the sefarim tie to the Gemara about keeping two Shabbosos. He then tells the Arvei Nachal's mashal of the king's servant whose two defenders, the king's children, are Shabbos and the Torah, and whom he must beg for forgiveness.

title.en: Honoring Shabbos with kedushah

summary.en: The Mashgiach's message: refraining from melachah is not enough; Shabbos, the princess, must be honored with kedushah, not with newspapers, books or idle talk. He brings the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mother and explains that Hashem's rest included rest from speech, and that Shabbos is a day of song with the malachim.

title.en: The cleansing power and hope for Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Yoma that Yom Kippur alone only suspends grave sins, and the Taz that together with Shabbos it atones for them fully. He closes with the Chazal that when nations prepare for war it is a time to expect Moshiach, and with brachos.

catalogTitle: לפי שהיה שורש הנס כל כך גבוה' היה כל כך בהסתר. התעוררות והלכות צניעות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Purim miracle came from so high and hidden a source that it had to stay concealed, and from this he draws a call to tznius and to the halachos of distancing from arayos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the garments Hashem made for Adam and Chava, explaining them as a reward for Adam covering Chava's shame, and as 'garments of light' that bring a surrounding light (or makif) like sukkah, tallis and tzitzis. He brings the Maharal: the Megillah has no open miracle because its root was too high to be revealed, which is why the redemption came through Esther, whose name speaks of hiddenness and who was a tzenuah, and through Mordechai, connected to the hidden ketores. Haman, rooted in the nachash, attacks through pritzus, as at Achashverosh's feast. The Mashgiach then reviews the halachos of distancing from arayos, links the Megillah's opening to a loss of Shabbos and of modest dress, and explains that clothing exists to cover a person's great inner light. He closes with Moshe Rabbeinu's hidden name in Tetzaveh and with preparing for Purim's hidden light through tznius and Torah.

en: Hashem made 'garments of light' for Adam and Chava as a reward for Adam covering Chava's shame instead of blaming her.
Some mitzvos bring an inner light that a person can contain, while the highest ones, like sukkah, the tallis and tzitzis, bring a surrounding light from above.
Following the Maharal, the Purim miracle was not open because its root was so high that it could not be revealed.
The redemption came through Esther and Mordechai, whose whole way was tznius and hiddenness.
The halachos of distancing from arayos are clear and apply to everyone, not only as a middas chassidus.
The purpose of clothing is to cover a person's great inner light, so styles made to attract defeat the purpose of a garment.
Purim is a concealed festival whose light is too great to be seen openly, like the hidden name of Moshe Rabbeinu in Parshas Tetzaveh.

title.en: Why Hashem made garments for Adam

summary.en: Starting from the priestly garments and the tzitz, the Mashgiach turns to the end of the Gan Eden story and asks why the naming of Chava interrupts, and why Hashem had to make garments for Adam and Chava when they had already made their own. He cites the Targumim that these were special garments of honor.

title.en: Adam calls Chava 'mother of all life'

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Adam, instead of blaming Chava for the destruction the sin brought, praised her as the mother of all life, and connects the name Chavah to 'chavos Ya'ir'. Because Adam covered her shame, Hashem in turn clothed them, measure for measure.

title.en: Garments of light: or pnimi and or makif

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that in Rabbi Meir's Torah it was written 'kosnos or' with an aleph, and explains the difference between mitzvos that bring an inner light and those that bring a surrounding light: sukkah, the sleeveless tallis, shemini and the eight threads of tzitzis with techeiles.

title.en: The Maharal: why the miracle was hidden

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Maharal's question why the Megillah has no open miracle, and his answer that the miracle came from so high a place that it could not be revealed. Therefore it came through Esther, a tzenuah, and Mordechai; Hashem's name is absent; and the greatness of Haman's klipah, in a time of galus within galus, required so high a salvation.

title.en: Above time; Esther, Mordechai and the ketores

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties Purim to the makif mitzvos and to matzah, which is made without time, showing the Megillah's rush at its climax. He explains Esther's tznius as inherited from Rachel, and Mordechai's hint in 'mor dror' and the ketores, a hidden avodah done in the Kodesh HaKodashim, making them a fitting pair.

title.en: Haman and the nachash; success through tznius

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Haman is hinted at in the tree of knowledge and that he stems from the nachash, who desired Chava. He shows that the Megillah opens with a feast of pritzus where Achashverosh lost Vashti, and teaches that every success of a person, including his destined match, depends on his guarding of tznius.

title.en: The sin of Achashverosh's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Jews were punished for enjoying Achashverosh's feast when the food was kosher, as each was served according to his wish. He answers that the feast's whole aim was pritzus, compares it to resorts of today, and brings another view that their sin was being present and taking it in; this leads into the halachos of distancing from arayos.

title.en: Halachos: distancing from arayos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Rambam's and the Shulchan Aruch's words that one must distance himself from women 'very, very much', explains the prohibition of any closeness to arayos, and stresses that nowadays every unmarried woman has the status of a niddah. He brings the Gemara on 'otzem einav meros bera' about not looking at women washing clothes at the river.

title.en: Touch, looking, and yehareg v'al ya'avor

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses touch derech chibah and the dispute between the Beis Yosef and the Shach, explains why medical care differs from shaking hands, and warns against looking even at a woman's clothes or walking behind her. He brings the Gemara of the lovesick man whom the Sages forbade even to speak with the woman, because the offshoots of giluy arayos are also yehareg v'al ya'avor.

title.en: Knesses Yisrael fallen; Achashverosh's stolen Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar on 'nafla lo sosif kum besulas Yisrael': in this galus only Hashem Himself will raise Knesses Yisrael. He brings the Midrash that Achashverosh could feast while the Beis HaMikdash lay in ruins because the Jews did not honor the oneg of Shabbos, so its gift passed to him, and asks who knows whether laxity in tznius delays Knesses Yisrael's rising.

title.en: Moshe's hidden name and the masked Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's name is absent from Tetzaveh because of 'mecheini na', and that through this he was united with a hidden light. Purim too comes masked because its light is too great; he compares drinking to an anesthetic before surgery, connects Mordechai as a spark of Moshe, and Yom Kippurim to Purim.

title.en: Tetzaveh: oil, eight garments, and Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects Tetzaveh to Purim: it opens with pure olive oil, a hint to the hidden part of the Torah that makes no sound, linked to the number eight, the eight priestly garments and the eight threads of tzitzis. He explains Haman as a hidden klipah, the fifty-amah gallows, and the Maharal on 'Haman min haTorah', and brings the Midrash that Adam's garments of light were the garments of the Kohen Gadol, which cover and protect.

title.en: Mordechai's royal garments and more covering

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Mordechai went out in royal garments of techeiles, and the Gemara that Yosef's gift of five changes of clothes to Binyamin hinted at Mordechai. He explains that each garment brings a surrounding light, brings Rabbi Pinchas of Koritz that Jews add garments when they daven, and explains why women need more covering than men.

title.en: The purpose of clothing is to cover

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person, made in the tzelem Elokim, holds great lights that must be hidden in garments, and the holier a place the more it must be covered. A garment's purpose is to cover, so styles made to attract are not garments; he brings the passuk in Yeshayahu about the haughty daughters of Tziyon and the Gemara's explanation of their conduct.

title.en: The seventh day: Vashti's fashions and lost zemiros

summary.en: On 'bayom hashevi'i k'tov lev hamelech bayayin' the Mashgiach brings that it was Shabbos, when Jews made kiddush and sang zemiros. He brings the Chasam Sofer that Vashti set immodest fashions which Jewish women followed, so they went to the party and the zemiros at home stopped, and he explains the decree that every man should rule his home in this light.

title.en: Preparing for Purim's hidden light

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes: on Purim a great hidden light fills the air, the light of Mordechai and Esther, likened to the neshamah yeseirah of Shabbos. To receive it one must take on tznius, keep away from the 'feast of Achashverosh' of the surrounding culture, and accept the Torah anew as the Jews did in 'kiymu v'kiblu'.

catalogTitle: “גם ושתי המלכה עשתה משתה נשים” - “להיות כל איש שורר בביתו”

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar, whose combination of Hashem's Name is hidden in the final letters of a passuk about the donkey, is the dark end-time when the 'feminine' force of the sitra achra rises, and that Vashti's party and Memuchan's decree, Purim's unity and a Jew's root in the 'beginning' turn it all around.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that each month has its own combination of Hashem's Name, and Adar's is hidden in the final letters of 'osri lagefen iro' (Bereishis 49:11). Through the Ohr HaChaim he explains that in the sitra achra the female is stronger than the male, and that before Moshiach this force rises, as the Megillah shows. Vashti's separate women's feast was a push for 'equality', and Memuchan's decree that every man rule his home, which the Gemara attributes to Haman and Tosfos' Midrash to Daniel, restored the right side over the left. He then builds on reishis and acharis: Israel is the true 'beginning', Amalek a false one; the last generations, like the last pesukim of the Torah, are bound to Bereishis. Adar is the month of earth and the donkey, yet a Jew's emunah comes from his root. He closes with Moshe's soul in every generation, unity through mishloach manos, and knocking on the gates of mercy on Purim.

en: Adar's combination of Hashem's Name lies in the final letters of 'osri lagefen iro... bnei asono', and the ending heh of 'iro' hints that in Adar the male yields to the female.
Following the Ohr HaChaim, in holiness the male is stronger, but in the sitra achra the female is stronger, and its final subjugation comes only with Moshiach.
The Megillah describes the period before the second Beis HaMikdash as a time like the footsteps of Moshiach, and Vashti's separate women's feast was the female force pushing for equality.

Memuchan's decree that every man rule his home strengthened the right side over the left; the Gemara says Memuchan was Haman and the Midrash in Tosfos says Daniel, and the Mashgiach explains both are true.
Israel is the true 'reishis', while Amalek is a false 'reishis' with no 'acharis'; the last generations, like the last pesukim of the Torah, are joined to Bereishis.
Even in the darkest time a Jew can believe, because 'Amen' is Kel Melech Ne'eman and he is rooted in Hashem Himself.
In Adar, the month Moshe was born, every Jew can connect to Moshe's soul, to good friends and to all of Klal Yisrael, and on Purim one should knock on the gates of mercy.

title.en: Adar's Name and the Ohr HaChaim's dream

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each month has a combination of Hashem's Name, and Adar's is in the final letters of 'osri lagefen iro'. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that the passuk speaks of two redemptions, and that in the sitra achra the female is stronger, illustrated by the Ohr HaChaim's own dream.

title.en: The female force before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that before Moshiach the female side of the sitra achra fights hardest, links the seven nations to the seven bad middos, and explains why Canaan corresponds to chesed. He then shows why 'iro' ends with a heh.

title.en: Adar as the end of days; Manoach and Shimshon

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Adar as the last, darkest part of the night before Nissan and the Megillah as the program of the footsteps of Moshiach. He explains that in holiness the man leads, why honoring one's wife comes from a different root, and how Manoach following his wife spoiled Shimshon's chance to be Moshiach.

title.en: Vashti's separate feast for women

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'gam Vashti hamalkah asesa mishteh nashim' as a separate convention of women demanding equal rights, and points out that the Megillah writes 'Vashti hamalkah' with her name before her title, showing her claim to equal rank.

title.en: Memuchan: Haman or Daniel?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Memuchan's advice that every man rule his home, the Gemara that Memuchan is Haman, and Tosfos citing a Midrash that he is Daniel, and asks why Tosfos mentions it. He explains that Vashti's success would have made din prevail over chesed above, so Hashem prepared the cure before the blow.

title.en: The court below rules, and Daniel's ruling

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the court below rules and the court above follows, with a story of the Ruzhiner and the Sanzer Rav. Daniel's ruling that every man rule his home was really a ruling for the heavenly court that the right side prevail, so the Gemara and the Midrash do not conflict.

title.en: Israel the true 'reishis', Amalek the false

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks on Rashi why the Torah begins with Bereishis and answers that Israel is called 'reishis'. Amalek is 'reishis goyim' but has no 'acharis', while the last pesukim of the Torah, which speak of the last generations, are joined to Bereishis.

title.en: The donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach ride the same donkey, the symbol of utter materialism, which tzaddikim subdue. He ties Amalek's claim to be 'reishis' to materialism and explains the sanctity of redeeming a firstborn donkey.

title.en: Amen, and reading the Megillah backwards

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Rabbi Chanina adds by saying 'Amen' stands for Kel Melech Ne'eman. He then explains that reading the Megillah draws down the same miracles each year, which is why reading it backwards is invalid, why Haman's ten sons fill a whole column, and how the plagues in the Haggadah work the same way.

title.en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon

summary.en: To explain Rabbi Yehuda's simanim, the Mashgiach retells the Gemara of the three Tannaim who spoke about Rome and brings the Chiddushei HaRim that they carried the souls of Yehuda, Yosef and Shimon, which explains each one's fate.

title.en: Four elements and burning the chametz

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the four letters of Hashem's Name, the four elements and the four camps, with Yehuda corresponding to fire, the root of all. From here he explains Rabbi Yehuda's view that chametz is destroyed only by burning, and why he gave simanim of initials for the plagues.

title.en: Emunah in the dark; Har HaBayis and Machpelah

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Adar the element of earth, a time of darkness, and answers the question on 'Amen': a Jew can believe because he is rooted in Kel Melech Ne'eman. He contrasts Har HaBayis as Israel's 'reishis' with Me'aras HaMachpelah as its 'acharis', both holding the same Adam and Avos.

title.en: Adar's final letters reversed; Moshe in every generation

summary.en: Returning to the opening, the Mashgiach explains why Adar's Name is in final letters about the donkey, and how Purim turns final letters into first letters. He then explains that Adar is the month of Moshe's passing and birth, that Moshe's soul is in every generation under another name, and why Moshe's name is absent from Tetzaveh.

title.en: Haman's thought of despair and its answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the despairing thought 'what connection do I have to Torah' is Haman's thought within a Jew. The answer is to strengthen oneself in emunah, connect to the root and to Moshe's soul, and feel newly born in Adar.

title.en: Mishloach manos as one great eruv

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges connecting with good friends, against Haman's 'mefuzar umeforad', and explains mishloach manos as an eruv joining all Jewish families into one. He adds that Purim's light is above the world and that Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim'.

title.en: Purim and the level of yechidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim's holiness is so great that one drinks until he cannot feel, and that on Purim all Jews rise to the level of yechidah, 'ish Yehudi' as 'ish yechidi'. He compares Purim's rhymes and music to a wedding and says Hashem Himself sends mishloach manos to every Jew.

title.en: The Gostininer knocks; Esther's request

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Gostininer became a great Rebbe by knocking on the Kotzker's door on Purim, and derives that on Purim one must knock on the gates of mercy. He closes with Esther's 'she'elasi uvakashasi' as the axis of the Megillah and Adar as a time of 'v'nahafoch'.

catalogTitle: ביאורי מהר"ל על מגילת אסתר - כל דבר שהוא יותר בקדושה הוא יותר בהסתרה. ועוד

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, largely following the Maharal, that the holier a thing is the more it must be hidden, and shows how the hidden miracle of Purim, Achashverosh's feast and the Megillah's message to the 'distant' all flow from this.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's allusion to Esther in 'haster astir': her salvation came from a hidden place, and the Purim miracles are greater precisely because they are concealed. Following the Maharal he links this to wine, to Binyamin as the last-born, to Yaakov's later emergence than Eisav, and to the hadas whose leaves cover its wood. Through Rabbi Pinchas of Koritz he ties the four parshiyos to the hidden light, which only tzaddikim can bear, and shows that every great holiness, from a sefer Torah to a Jew's head, needs more covering. The Megillah hides Hashem's name, yet 'the King' alludes to Him and Achashverosh's kingdom mirrors the heavenly one. Achashverosh's feast celebrated the end of the seventy years without redemption; the Jews' sin was rejoicing that kingship stayed in exile. He ends with the king who values the distant pearl, and Adar as the month of the distant.

en: The Mashgiach teaches that the greater the holiness of a thing, the more it must be hidden and covered, and that the Purim miracles are greater because they come in concealment.
The hidden light of creation rests in Shabbos, in the Torah and in Moshe Rabbeinu, and it shines especially on the Shabbosos of the four parshiyos, when two sifrei Torah are taken out.
The Megillah never names Hashem, yet 'the King' in it alludes to Him, and Achashverosh's rule over 127 provinces mirrors the structure of the heavenly kingdom.
Achashverosh's feast celebrated his belief that the seventy years had ended without redemption, so that kingship would remain with him rather than return to Yerushalayim.
The food at the feast was kosher; the Jews' sin was that by attending they rejoiced that kingship remained in exile, a disgrace to the honor of Heaven, and they repented by fasting.
The Megillah was written for a people in exile who feel far from Hashem, to show that He is with them even in concealment and that the service of the distant is especially precious to Him.

the near and the distant (kerovim and rechokim)

title.en: Esther: salvation from a hidden place

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's allusion to Esther in 'haster astir' and explains that some salvations come from a hidden source, and that the Purim miracles are greater because they are concealed. With the Maharal he connects this to wine, to Binyamin as the last tribe born, to Yaakov emerging after Eisav, and to the hadas whose leaves cover its wood.

title.en: The hidden light, Shabbos and the Torah

summary.en: Through Rabbi Pinchas of Koritz the Mashgiach links the four parshiyos to the hidden light, which only tzaddikim can bear and which the wicked cannot tolerate on Shabbos. He shows that Moshe Rabbeinu, Shabbos and the Torah all share this light, and explains why a sefer must not be left open.

title.en: More holiness needs more covering

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Jews add garments for davening and before a great man, cover the head, wear a gartel, and wrap the sefer Torah, because greater holiness needs greater protection; he brings the Gemara's story of the boy whose covered head guarded him. He ties the reading of the mishkan's coverings to Adar and explains the extra sifrei Torah on the four parshiyos and on Simchas Torah.

title.en: The hidden King of the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Megillah never mentions Hashem's name, yet a great chesed came down hidden; therefore shalach manos is covered. 'The King' in the Megillah alludes to Hashem, earthly kingship mirrors heavenly kingship, and the Maharal explains Achashverosh's 127 provinces as seven, twenty and one hundred, corresponding to three worlds.

title.en: The seventy-year reckoning

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the Persians knew of the prophecy that the Beis Hamikdash would be rebuilt after seventy years; Belshazzar miscalculated, used the Temple vessels and was killed, and Achashverosh made his own reckoning. He explains that the nations, deep inside, sense that there is a Creator and fear the prophecy.

title.en: No one knows the time of redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach says even Daniel erred in the reckoning, and brings the Rambam that Rabbi Akiva thought Bar Koziva was Moshiach: no one can reveal the time of redemption. Achashverosh, sensing that the return of kingship to Yerushalayim would end his own, celebrated in the third year; the Mashgiach then brings the Gemara that the Jews were liable for enjoying that feast.

title.en: Kosher food, but a feast of exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the sin was, since Chazal make clear the food was kosher and each guest got what he wished. He answers that the feast celebrated kingship staying with the nations; joining it meant rejoicing in the exile of malchus, a disgrace to the honor of Heaven. The Jews repented by fasting, and so Purim is celebrated with a great feast; he contrasts Achashverosh's kingdom with Shlomo HaMelech's.

title.en: Achashverosh's imitation throne

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Megillah is eternal: in every generation there is an Achashverosh with a feast that may be kosher, yet the kingdom is theirs. He brings the Midrash and Targum Sheni that Achashverosh tried to copy Shlomo's throne, which symbolized Hashem's kingship, and produced only a cheap imitation; the angels protested the feast, and Hashem answered with days corresponding to days, because Jews had desecrated Shabbos.

title.en: The far ones first: the king's pearl

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute of Rav and Shmuel whether inviting the distant first made Achashverosh wise or foolish, asks how either could call the other's view foolish, and explains with the Maharal that they disagree whether kingship is shown more through the far or the near. He brings the mashal from Sidduro shel Shabbos of the king who valued a pearl from the deep above diamonds, and applies it to the service of one who was far.

title.en: Adar, the month of the distant

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai's letters 'to the near and the far' are addressed above all to the distant, and that Adar is the month of the distant. The Megillah was written for a people in exile to show that Hashem works miracles even in hiddenness; it opens with a feast because in Heaven the main feast is for the distant, whose small service in exile is dearer than the great avodah of Temple times.

catalogTitle: The מקוה of יו”כ Reveals the Essence of Good in Every Yid

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur, the fortieth day of teshuvah, is a mikveh in time in which every Jew reaches the hidden point of good from Avraham Avinu in his heart, and Hashem Himself cleanses him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the last Mishnah of Yoma: Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time, and Hashem Himself is the mikveh. He builds on the number forty: an embryo is formed in forty days, and the Chiddushei HaRim teaches that in every Jew's heart there is one hidden point, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, that evil never reaches, which is why Hashem is called 'Magen Avraham'. This explains the Rambam on a person coerced to say 'I want', and why a sinner receives only thirty-nine lashes, Adam received thirty-nine curses, and the generation of the desert was spared in the fortieth year. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul end on Yom Kippur, the fortieth se'ah of the mikveh, when a Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his own heart. Through the Yismach Moshe's parable of a stained suit he teaches that Hashem removes what our teshuvah cannot, and he closes that Yom Kippur is a joyous day to be cherished.

en: Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time, and on it Hashem Himself is the mikveh who cleanses a Jew of his sins.
Following the Chiddushei HaRim, every Jew has one hidden point in his heart, inherited from Avraham Avinu, that evil cannot reach, and there he wants to be a tzaddik.
A sinner receives thirty-nine lashes rather than forty because his fortieth point never agreed to the sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul culminate on Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, when the mikveh of forty se'ah is complete and a Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his heart.
A Jew must do teshuvah as far as he can, and Hashem removes the stains he cannot remove himself.
Yom Kippur is an awesome day but also a joyous one, and one should cherish every minute of it rather than count the hours until the fast ends.
