forty days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul
the Holy of Holies in the heart

title.en: Yom Kippur as a mikveh, and the number forty

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the last Mishnah of Yoma, 'Ashreichem Yisrael' and 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem', and explains that Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time in which Hashem Himself cleanses a Jew. He then introduces the forty days in which an embryo is formed, bringing the Gemara in Berachos and Rashi on the forty days of the Mabul.

title.en: The hidden point of Avraham in every heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah says forty lashes while only thirty-nine are given, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim on 'Magen Avraham': in every Jew there is a hidden point from Avraham Avinu that evil cannot reach. With this he explains the Rambam on a person who is beaten until he says 'I want' to bring his korban.

title.en: Thirty-nine lashes, curses and melachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that a sinner receives only thirty-nine lashes because his fortieth point protested the sin. He applies the same idea to the thirty-nine curses after the sin of Adam, which are the source of the thirty-nine melachos forbidden on Shabbos, and to the generation of the desert who were all spared in the fortieth year.

title.en: The fortieth day and the inner Holy of Holies

summary.en: The Mashgiach counts the forty days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, when the Satan has no power. As the Kohen Gadol enters the Holy of Holies, every Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his heart, especially at Ne'ilah, where no angel and no Satan can enter.

title.en: The fortieth se'ah completes the mikveh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that a kosher mikveh needs forty se'ah: each day of Elul adds a se'ah, and on Yom Kippur the mikveh is complete. The climax of the Avodah recited in Musaf is the Kohen Gadol's entry into the Holy of Holies, and so too every Jew reaches his pure yetzer tov and resolves to be good for the coming year.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's parable of the stained suit

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Yismach Moshe's parable of a man whose suit for an audience with the king was stained with tar, which only an expert could fully clean. Teshuvah cannot remove every stain, he explains, but Hashem is the expert who does the rest, as in the case of someone who cannot recall whom he wronged; he urges saying at least the forgiveness lines of Tefillah Zakah.

title.en: Yom Kippur, an awesome and joyous day

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Yom Kippur is awesome but also a happy day: in place of physical pleasures it has five tefillos full of delight, in which Hashem speaks back to the Jew and says He erases his sins like a cloud. He criticizes those who watch the clock waiting to eat; one should hold on to every minute.

title.en: Chaim and Yankel, and closing brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Chaim, who enjoys Yom Kippur, with Yankel, who keeps checking his watch; both eat at the same time, but Yankel spoiled his Yom Kippur, as the Yesod v'Shoresh HaAvodah writes. He sums up that one must do teshuvah yet feel fortunate to have Yom Kippur, and closes with brachos for a good inscription and the Geulah.

catalogTitle: הכנה לשבת ע"י קדושת יסוד כמו שנלמד מהמגילה. (שייכות לזכור)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows from the Megillah that a true Shabbos comes only through preparation in the six weekdays and through kedushas haBris (the holiness of Yesod), the opposite of Amalek, and that Purim is the time to wage that war and receive the Torah anew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the two mitzvos of remembering, Zachor of Shabbos and Zachor of Amalek, and asks why one is remembered constantly and the other only once a year. Shabbos must be prepared all week; the Shabbos a person has depends on his week. He then explains that the root of Shabbos is Yesod, the holiness of the Bris, the attribute of Yosef HaTzaddik and of the sixth day, while Amalek is its opposite. From the Gemara in Megillah on the seven officers of Achashverosh, whose names allude to korbanos, he focuses on Memuchan, linked to the Table and the lechem hapanim, which was baked on Friday because it is part of the building of the Mishkan. Achashverosh, without preparation, could only reach a Shabbos of wine. The Mashgiach then speaks of Purim's hidden greatness, the war with Amalek inside the heart, the neshamah of Moshe Rabbeinu in Adar, the revelation at the Megillah reading, and kiymu v'kiblu.

en: Remembering Shabbos is a constant obligation, while remembering Amalek is done once a year, because Shabbos is remembered to sanctify it and Amalek to erase it.
Shabbos does not come by itself: the Shabbos a person has is shaped by his Torah, mitzvos and avodah during the week.
The way to Shabbos is kedushas haBris, the attribute of Yesod and of Yosef HaTzaddik, which corresponds to the sixth day, the day of preparation.
Amalek is the opposite of kedushas haBris, and wiping out Amalek through teshuvah is what opens the way to a holy Shabbos.
The lechem hapanim is part of the building of the Table and the Mishkan, which is why its baking does not override Shabbos and it must be prepared on Friday.
Purim is a gift beyond comprehension in which all Jews become one, and it is the time to fight the inner Amalek and to accept the Torah anew.

candidateTopics: zachor of Shabbos and zachor of Amalek
kedushas habris and the attribute of yesod
Purim and the war with Amalek

title.en: Two kinds of Zachor: Shabbos and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Zachor of Shabbos is a daily mitzvah while Zachor of Amalek is once a year, and brings a pshat he saw from Satmar. He explains that holy words and thoughts draw kedushah and that even thoughts of one's sins should be limited, and concludes that Shabbos must be built all week.

title.en: Preparing all week for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Romanover's teaching that Shabbos receives its quality from the weekdays, and explains Zachor as remembering in every test of the week that Shabbos is coming, and making a Shabbos worth remembering. He ends with the mitzvah to prepare on Friday, 'v'haya bayom hashishi v'heichinu'.

title.en: The seven tzaddikim and Yosef HaTzaddik

summary.en: At someone's request the Mashgiach turns to the seven tzaddikim who correspond to the seven middos, and explains that only Yosef is called 'tzaddik' because he withstood the test of kedushah. He brings the Midrash that in Yosef's merit only one woman, Shlomis bas Divri, stumbled in Egypt.

title.en: Bereishis: the Bris and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that 'Bereishis' contains both 'bris esh' and 'yarei Shabbos', teaching that one merits Shabbos through kedushas haBris, and links Friday to Yesod and to guarding the eyes. He then shows that Amalek, who attacked the Bris, is the opposite of Zachor of Shabbos.

title.en: Erasing Amalek to merit Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash of the cup of wine and the cup of vinegar to explain the link between the two Zachors: one who wipes out Amalek through teshuvah merits a holy Shabbos. He mentions the custom of teshuvah and staying up on Thursday night before Shabbos, and urges being in the beis medrash on Friday.

title.en: Achashverosh's officers and the korbanos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Megillah that the names of the seven officers allude to korbanos the angels mentioned in defense of Israel, and asks what Memuchan alludes to; he reads it as the Table prepared for the lechem hapanim. He adds the Gemara that Memuchan is Haman and asks why he is called by that name.

title.en: Why the lechem hapanim is baked before Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why baking the lechem hapanim does not override Shabbos like other korbanos, and why the Torah puts 'lechem panim lefanai tamid' in Parshas Terumah. He answers that the lechem hapanim is part of the building of the Table, so removing it even for a moment would break the Shulchan, and building the Mishkan does not override Shabbos.

title.en: On Shabbos every Jew is a Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach reconciles the views on whether the Mishkan was commanded before or after the sin of the Golden Calf: without sin every Jew would be a Mishkan, and on Shabbos he is. Therefore the kohanim eat the lechem hapanim, part of the Mishkan, on Shabbos; its six-and-six arrangement and its freshness point to the sixth day and to Yosef's attribute of Yesod.

title.en: Achashverosh's Shabbos of wine

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yaaros Devash that by mazal Shabbos is a hard day for the nations, while Jews rise above mazal. That is why Achashverosh, on the seventh day, had to lift his spirits with wine, 'k'tov lev hamelech bayayin', a forced cheer rather than true goodness of heart.

title.en: Seven maidens, seven officers, seven days

summary.en: From Esther's seven maidens, by whom she counted the days of the week, the Mashgiach shows that sevens in the Megillah hide the seven days of creation, so the seventh officer, Memuchan, corresponds to Shabbos and its preparation. Without preparation there is no Shabbos, and Memuchan's 'preparation' was the opposite, in tumah.

title.en: The hidden greatness of Purim

summary.en: Turning to Purim, the Mashgiach explains that Purim is beyond human grasp, which is why one drinks until 'lo yada', like anesthesia before surgery. Purim is the seventh festival and includes all the others; when all Jews join together they have the power of a tzaddik, as in 'kenos es kol haYehudim'. He tells of a tzaddik who read 'Napoleon' in the Megillah.

title.en: The inner war with Amalek in Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who values every moment of Purim can connect to it, and that the time before Purim is the time to fight Amalek, who today hides inside the heart through blemish of the Bris. He links this to Adar, to the incomplete Name until Amalek is erased, and to the neshamah of Moshe Rabbeinu revealed in Mordechai, culminating in kiymu v'kiblu.

title.en: The hidden world revealed at the Megillah reading

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the sefer Yesod Yosef that there is an awesome hidden world, the root of Mordechai's soul, that is revealed only on Purim from the Megillah reading on. The brachah 'al mikra Megillah' is read as calling out that revelation, so one should answer amen with great kavanah and awe.

title.en: Purim as a special treat in exile

summary.en: With a memory of receiving oranges as a sick child, the Mashgiach explains that Purim is a special gift Hashem gives the Jews in exile, after losing the Beis HaMikdash. Its essence is love of every Jew, shown in mishloach manos, and he urges making peace with friends on Erev Purim.

title.en: From the passing of Moshe to his birth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a spark of Moshe Rabbeinu; sin is a 'passing of Moshe' within him, and teshuvah in Adar brings a 'birth of Moshe' on a higher level. He closes with a brachah for kiymu v'kiblu, good Shabbosos, erasing Amalek, and the final redemption.

catalogTitle: דרוש והתעוררות: חודש הכולל' יום שהוא למעלה מהשגתינו' מצוות היום

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the war against Amalek needs a power that includes all of Klal Yisrael, which Shaul in his humility sought through the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, and which Purim in Adar Sheni, the month that includes all months, brings down as a light beyond understanding.

abstract.en: Opening with the Chasam Sofer's call to explain Purim to the people, the Mashgiach turns to the haftarah of Shaul and Amalek and asks why Shmuel first reminds Shaul that he was anointed king, and what Shaul meant by claiming he fulfilled Hashem's word and by answering that he kept the animals for sacrifices. He builds an answer from the order of the three mitzvos on entering the land: a king, who includes the whole nation, is needed to fight Amalek, who includes all impurity. Through Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh, the avos and the shevatim, and the stones of the choshen, he shows that Binyamin, whose stone lacks the names of the avos, holds the unity of the mizbeach. Shaul, too humble to see himself as king, sought that power through korbanos. Adar Sheni includes all months, so Haman's lottery failed. The Mashgiach ends with the light revealed at the Megillah reading and the mitzvos of the day.

en: The war against Amalek, who includes all impurity, needs a king, who includes the whole nation; this is why appointing a king comes before wiping out Amalek and building the Beis HaMikdash.

Shabbos is the unity of the avos, while Rosh Chodesh and the twelve months correspond to the shevatim, the branches; the stones of the choshen belong to the shevatim, yet the names of the avos engraved on them bring in unity.
Binyamin's stone carries none of the letters of the avos, because Binyamin himself is the unity of Klal Yisrael: the mizbeach stands in his portion.
Shaul, out of humility, did not consider himself a true king, so he sought the all-including power through the mizbeach by taking the animals of Amalek for korbanos.

Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month, includes all the months, so the war against Haman took place in it, and Haman's lottery erred in seeing Adar only as Binyamin's month and the month of Moshe's passing.
At the reading of the Megillah a hidden and awesome world is revealed once a year, from which all salvations come.

candidateTopics: Adar Sheni as the all-including month
Shaul and the war against Amalek
appointing a king before wiping out Amalek

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's call to explain Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying Purim is a day nobody understands, and reads from the Chasam Sofer that the people celebrate without knowing what Purim is, so the sages used to gather them and explain it. He excuses his own speaking with the Chofetz Chaim's parable of the peasant who brought dirty water to put out a fire in the king's palace.

title.en: Shaul and Amalek in the haftarah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the haftarah and asks why Shmuel prefaces the command to fight Amalek with 'Hashem sent me to anoint you king'. He retells how Shaul spared Agag and the animals and then told Shmuel he had fulfilled Hashem's word, and notes that from Agag's one night came Haman and the miracle of Purim.

title.en: Shaul's puzzling answers to Shmuel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Shaul could claim he fulfilled Hashem's word, and what kind of reply 'to bring korbanos' is to Shmuel's 'though you are small in your eyes, you are the head of the tribes of Israel'. He explains Shaul's later excuse, 'I feared the people', as referring to Doeg, who was considered equal to the whole nation.

title.en: Three mitzvos and the gift of the nesi'im

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that three mitzvos were commanded on entering the land, a king, wiping out Amalek and building the Beis HaMikdash, and asks why a king must come before Amalek. He then turns to the nesi'im who brought the shoham and milu'im stones, with Rashi's criticism that they waited to complete what was missing.

title.en: Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh, avos and shevatim

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Shabbos, fixed by Hashem and corresponding to the avos and to unity, with Rosh Chodesh and the twelve months, which correspond to the shevatim, the branches of the tree. The Mikdash and Yerushalayim are of the aspect of Shabbos, while the twelve stones of the choshen, each in its tribe's color, belong to the shevatim.

title.en: The choshen stones and Binyamin's mizbeach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the stones, which belong to the shevatim, are counted among the Mishkan's donations, and answers with the Gemara that 'Avraham Yitzchak Yaakov shivtei Yeshurun' was engraved on them, six letters to a stone. Binyamin's stone gets none of those letters, and the Mashgiach explains that Binyamin needs none: the mizbeach, which unites all of Klal Yisrael, stands in his portion.

title.en: Moshe and Bilaam, the king and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer on 'no prophet arose in Israel like Moshe': Moshe included all of Klal Yisrael, so he had to stand in tefillah during the war with Amalek, who includes all impurity and is bound up with Bilaam. From this he explains why a king, who includes the whole nation, must be appointed before the war on Amalek and the building of the Mikdash.

title.en: Shaul's humility and his korbanos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shaul, who hid among the vessels and saw himself as coming from Binyamin, the last tribe, did not believe he was truly king and lacked the all-including power. He therefore took the animals of Amalek as korbanos for the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, to draw that power from it; Shmuel's words 'you are the head of the tribes of Israel' answer him, and 'I feared the people' meant his regard for Doeg.

title.en: Adar Sheni, the all-including month

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month, includes all months, so the war against Haman happened in it. Haman's lottery saw Adar as Binyamin's month without the power of the avos and as the month Moshe died, but he did not know Mordechai was a spark of Moshe, and the Gemara reads the names of the advisors around Achashverosh as a list of korbanos, the power of Binyamin's mizbeach.

title.en: Purim as a renewed kabbalas haTorah

summary.en: Turning to Purim itself, the Mashgiach says it is like Shavuos, a renewed acceptance of the Torah with love, with three days of preparation before it. Purim carries the power of Shabbos and more: the extra soul that comes for moments at the Kedushah of Shabbos is present the whole day of Purim, beginning with the Megillah.

title.en: The awesome world revealed at the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the sefer Yesod Yosef that a hidden, awesome world is revealed only once a year, at the reading of the Megillah, and explains with the Alter Rebbe's siddur that a goral is above reason, which links Purim to Yom Kippur. Because the Megillah comes from so high a place it has no Name of Hashem and will never be nullified; one who reads it as past history does not fulfill the mitzvah, for its salvations happen anew each year.

title.en: Mishloach manos, matanos and the seudah

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the mitzvos of the day: in sending mishloach manos a Jew arouses Hashem to send him portions, tzedakah on Purim rises to a higher world, and the drinking must not disturb others. He reads the Kedushas Levi that the Purim seudah should be eaten with joy in accepting the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, and compares each bite to taking a vitamin that brings in that strength.

title.en: From Purim to Pesach; Mordechai at every seudah

summary.en: The Mashgiach quotes the Stoliner Rebbe that as Purim goes, so goes Pesach, and the Chesed L'Avraham that the thirty days before Pesach, beginning with Purim, start Hashem's taking Jews out of impurity. He describes all the Purim seudos as one seudah of unity, tells of Mordechai HaTzaddik appearing at Reb Pinchas of Koretz's seudah, and closes that Purim is above comprehension and above all the festivals.

catalogTitle: המתיקות' הקדושה והאורות של "האגרת הזאת"

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah is a personal letter, an iggeres, sent to every Jew, spread open with lights that come down to even the lowest generation, so that Purim can bring great salvation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that the Gemara expounds the Megillah at length, as it does for no other Yom Tov, and that people celebrate Purim without knowing what it is. Through stories of R' Elazar of Amsterdam and the Slonimer Rebbe he shows that Purim, when Hashem comes down to us as Yom Kippur raises us up, is a day to bring salvation. Each tzaddik serves Purim by his own root, yet all roots meet in the Megillah. Its lights exceed even Shabbos, but they are hidden, and Hashem loves those who serve Him in hiddenness. The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter addressed to each Jew, and unlike other lofty mitzvos that are kept covered, it is spread open so its lights reach the world. After the Spinka story of a soul that found its tikkun through a Megillah read on Pesach, he teaches that each lower generation's Purim is greater, and calls for a battle of Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

en: On Yom Kippur a Jew must rise up to Hashem, while on Purim Hashem comes down to the Jews, even into the place of exile.
Each tzaddik and each Jew serves Hashem on Purim according to the root of his soul, but all the roots come together in the Megillah.
The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter, because it was written to every single Jew personally.
Lofty mitzvos such as the shofar, the challos and the matzos are kept covered, but the Megillah is spread out entirely, so that its lights spread through the world.
Since Purim's nature is to come down to the lowest levels, the Purim of a lower generation is greater than any before it.
Purim is a battle, and the Jews' weapons in it are Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: Why one must speak about Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Gemara expounds the Megillah like a midrash, as it does for no other Yom Tov, and brings the Chasam Sofer that people celebrate Purim without knowing what it is. He tells how R' Elazar of Amsterdam brought salvation on Purim through drinking and dancing rather than Tehillim.

title.en: Purim brings salvation in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim joins miracle and nature, and is a weekday Yom Tov of exile; citing the Zohar, he says that on Purim Hashem comes down to the Jews as on Yom Kippur they rise to Him. He tells of the Slonimer Rebbe's extra Purim seudah for the sake of salvation, and says Purim must bring salvation now, when Jewish blood is being spilled.

title.en: Each tzaddik serves Purim by his root

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how differently tzaddikim conducted Purim, from Slonim to Komarna, and brings the Chasam Sofer on the separate gate of each tribe to show that every soul has its own root, yet all roots meet in the Megillah and in Mordechai. He tells how the Avnei Nezer's father merited his son by learning all Purim, and warns against jumping from one avodah to another.

title.en: The hidden lights of the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kedushas Levi and the Chasam Sofer that the light of Megillas Esther is greater than that of the Torah of Moshe, and explains that Purim's lights exceed even Shabbos but are clothed and hidden. Citing R' Yitzchak of Vorka, he calls the days the Megillah may be read early the three days of preparation before a kabbalas haTorah of love.

title.en: Keser malchus for a generation of hiddenness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem loves the generation of hiddenness, in which the sweetness of serving Him has been taken away, and contrasts it with earlier Chassidim, such as a Chabadnik who davened until four in the afternoon with tears. Whoever serves Him without that sweetness is like Esther and merits keser malchus; citing the Avodas Yisroel, he adds that Purim is like Shabbos.

title.en: The Megillah as a personal letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Megillah is called both a sefer and an iggeres: a sefer is written for whoever wants to buy it, while a letter is sealed and addressed to one person. Every Jew receives the Megillah from Mordechai and Esther as a private letter, like a yeshiva bochur reading his parents' news that his baby brother has grown an inch.

title.en: Covered mitzvos and the spread-out Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that mitzvos from a higher world are kept covered: the shofar, the Shabbos challos, the matzos (covered all Pesach in Chernobyl) and the Sefer Torah. The Megillah, though from a high world, is spread out entirely like a letter, and citing the Kozhnitzer Maggid he explains that this reveals the hidden and spreads its lights over all creation.

title.en: Moshiach, the wine of Purim and asking for all

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Mordechai is a bechinah of Moshiach and the Megillah will be understood only when Moshiach comes, and that the Purim seudah resembles the feast of the future. The wine of Purim is a higher wine than that of Shabbos Kiddush, and since Hashem tells Esther 'what is your request', on Purim one may ask for everything; even a simple Jew can rise to a tzaddik's heichal.

title.en: The Spinka story: Purim on Pesach night

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story the Imrei Yosef of Spinka told about 'a young man': reading the Megillah on the second night of Pesach, he was approached by a soul that had missed its Purim tikkun. The heavenly court asked him whether that night could be Purim, and he ruled that since Haman was hanged on Pesach, it could, and the soul received its tikkun.

title.en: The greatest Purim and the call to battle

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that as the world falls lower each year, Purim, which comes down to us, grows greater, and tells how Mordechai came to rejoice with a lonely tzaddik. Citing the Rosh, he compares Ta'anis Esther to Moshe's tefillah in the war with Amalek, and closes that Purim is a battle to be fought with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

catalogTitle: Subordinating Ourselves to Hashem on these Holy Days

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that bowing down on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is total subordination to Hashem as King, possible outside the Beis HaMikdash only because these ten days are the Beis HaMikdash in time, and that when a Jew bows, all of creation bows with him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the greatness of Yom Kippur, the Shabbos of all Shabbosim, when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim and every Jew rises to the level of the angels. Leaving the main themes to the boys' own rebbeim, he takes one small custom: falling prostrate in the davening. Bowing means surrendering one's existence before the King, and the Ba'al HaTanya writes that this is possible only in the Beis HaMikdash, the place of Malchus. Why then do we bow on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur? Using the Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of place, time and soul, the Mashgiach explains that the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time: the King comes to us. He then describes the world before Adam's sin, Adam's call to all creatures to bow, and the power of a Jew's bowing and teshuvah to move all creation, ending with the dog's song in Perek Shirah.

en: Hishtachavayah, falling prostrate, means total subordination to Hashem as King, to the point of surrendering one's own existence.
Such total subordination belongs to the Beis HaMikdash, the place of Malchus, so outside it bowing would not be real.
The ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time, so on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to us and we may bow wherever we are.
On these days we ask Hashem to bring back the world as it was before Adam's sin, when all creation accepted His kingship.
A Jew's teshuvah and bowing move the whole creation, because all of creation is connected with the Jewish people.

title.en: The greatness of Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Yom Kippur as the Shabbos of all Shabbosim, a day like the World to Come when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim on behalf of all Jews. He lists its main themes, fasting, teshuvah, vidui and appeasing others, and says he will instead explain one small custom of the day.

title.en: Bowing before the King

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the falling prostrate of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur means, and explains that in these days, when Hashem is near, His kingship is present and bowing is total self-nullification before the King. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya that such bowing is possible only in the Beis HaMikdash, and asks why we bow on these days.

title.en: The Beis HaMikdash in time

summary.en: Using the Sefer Yetzirah's teaching that creation is made in place, time and soul, the Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the calendar and the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time. Malchus comes to us, which is why we bow, why there is no mitzvah to go up to Yerushalayim on Yom Kippur, and why the chazzan calls out HaMelech from where he stands.

title.en: Adam's world and the window-shade string

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the world at Adam's creation, when everything accepted Hashem's kingship, which we ask to restore on these days. He tells of Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz holding a window-shade string during Shemoneh Esrei of Rosh Hashanah, and brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Adam called all creatures to bow, and they did.

title.en: The power of a Jew's teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that a Jew does not realize how powerful he is: his teshuvah moves all creatures and other Jews far away, because everything is connected to the Jewish people, as the passuk says everything was put under Adam's feet. When he bows on Yom Kippur and declares he has no wish but Hashem's, all creation bows with him, like one button lighting a whole tower.

title.en: The dog's song in Perek Shirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Perek Shirah, where every creature has a passuk of song, and asks why the dog says the same words Adam used to call creation to bow. He explains why the dog is a term of contempt: it is not independent and is happy with a substitute master, while true freedom is to serve Hashem alone. He then returns to Adam's call.

catalogTitle: גודל כח היום; הדרכה איך לנהוג בו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach describes the great power of Purim, a day of turning around and of accepting the Torah with love whose holiness lasts all day, and guides how to keep it: with joy, with kavanah in its foods, without drunkenness, and with tefillah for every yeshuah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Megillah's twice-mentioned 'turning over' and says Adar is a time when a person can turn himself around, daven for Klal Yisrael, and draw on the strong mazal of Adar. He explains that the days before Purim are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos, because on Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah willingly, and brings the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's holiness exceeds even the Torah of Moshe. The kedushah of Keser stays all Purim day, and Purim is greater than Yom Kippur, so it must be met with joy. He then teaches that holy foods become part of a person, warns sharply against drunkenness, explains why the Megillah is opened entirely, and answers why tzaddikim did not ask for the redemption on Purim. A story of the Shomer Emunim shows Purim's power for yeshuos.

en: Adar is a month of 'turning over', when a person can turn himself around: daven, learn and fix his middos.
On Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah with love, so the days before it are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos.
The kedushah of Keser, present on Shabbos only during Kedushah of Musaf, remains the whole day of Purim, and no accuser has a hold then.
The foods of Shabbos and Yom Tov carry the holiness of the day and become part of the person who eats them with kavanah.
Drinking on Purim should be a glass of wine and a short nap; getting drunk is a disgrace and causes chillul Hashem.
Everything one needs can be drawn from the Megillah, and on Purim tzaddikim have permission to bring yeshuos they cannot bring all year.

title.en: Adar, the month of turning over

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Megillah speaks of 'turning over' twice, for the day and for the month, and says a person can use Adar to turn himself around. He adds that tefillos are accepted from Adar to Sivan, urges davening for Klal Yisrael in its danger, and brings the Gemara that a Jew's mazal is strong in Adar.

title.en: Three days of preparation before Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Mishnah's days for reading the Megillah and the walled cities, then explains that the three days before Purim are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, because on Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah willingly and with love.

title.en: The kedushah of Keser all Purim day

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah is holier than the Torah of Moshe, the Mashgiach explains that the kedushah of Keser stays all Purim day, that Purim is greater than Yom Kippur, and that Purim must therefore be met with great joy, not with tension.

title.en: Purim is not a holiday of wildness; holy foods

summary.en: The Mashgiach rejects the view of Purim as a Jewish version of the gentiles' wild holiday, and through a parable of an egg that 'needs mazal' to end up in a Jewish Shabbos dish, he describes the fixed Shabbos foods and the special Purim foods as holding great secrets, to be eaten with kavanah.

title.en: What one eats becomes part of him

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that unlike other mitzvos, food becomes part of the person; this is why forbidden foods are so grave, and why each Yom Tov has its food: matzah on Pesach, dairy on Shavuos, eating in the sukkah, holishkes on Simchas Torah, latkes on Chanukah and hamantaschen on Purim.

title.en: The Purim seudah and the danger of drunkenness

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the seudah and wine are an obligation, but getting drunk is not for this generation: most tzaddikim drank a glass of wine, the Satmar Rav was an exception whose drunkenness revealed hidden Torah, and the poskim say to drink a little and nap. He describes the disgrace and chillul Hashem of drunkenness, from Adam and Noach to today's emergency rooms.

title.en: The open Megillah and its yeshuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Sefer Torah, kept covered, with the Megillah, opened entirely before reading so its holiness spreads to the whole world, and shows that every kind of yeshuah is found in the Megillah. He adds that Purim is like Shabbos, so one wears Shabbos clothes, and that at the seudah all yeshuos can be drawn.

title.en: Why tzaddikim did not ask for the geulah; the ke'arah

summary.en: Reading 'what is your request' as Hashem asking Klal Yisrael on Purim, the Mashgiach asks why great tzaddikim did not ask for the geulah, and answers that they were shown the purpose of galus. He tells how the Shomer Emunim on Purim promised children for a silver ke'arah, says every Jew can enter the Holy of Holies on Purim, and closes with practical words for the day.

catalogTitle: ביטול קליפת עמלק של "רפו ידיהם מן התורה"

oneLiner.en: Before Purim, the Mashgiach explains that Torah learned with love sweetens harsh decrees, that Amalek's power is the slackening and cooling toward Torah, and calls on his community to strengthen fixed learning, davening together and daily mussar.

abstract.en: Following the Chasam Sofer's custom of speaking before Purim, the Mashgiach compares Adar, especially the second Adar, to Elul as a month of teshuvah. He asks why Rashi on the verse 'what did they see… and what came upon them' departs from the Gemara's reading. Bringing the Ohr HaChaim, he explains that Torah learned with love and awe rises to Binah and sweetens judgments, which otherwise are sweetened by the passing of tzaddikim, as with Avishai ben Tzeruyah. Following the Chasam Sofer, Mordechai and Esther meant to give their lives as an atonement; the result was 'kiymu v'kiblu', Torah with love, which made that unnecessary. Amalek attacked at Refidim, when hands slackened from Torah, and he cools a person off. The Mashgiach proposes an hour of learning before Maariv, brings the Yismach Yisrael's takanos on learning and davening together, warns about assimilation, tells two stories, and urges daily mussar.

en: Adar, the last month counted from Nissan, is a month of teshuvah like Elul, and the second Adar of a leap year even more so.
Torah learned with love and awe of Hashem rises to Binah, the root of all judgments, and sweetens them there.
Mordechai's and Esther's self-sacrifice brought about 'kiymu v'kiblu', the Jews' acceptance of the Torah with love, which is the answer to 'what came upon them'.
Amalek's strength comes from 'Refidim', the slackening of hands from Torah, and his effect is to cool a person off.
The Mashgiach proposes that whoever can should come to the beis medrash and learn for an hour before Maariv, as a commitment without a vow.
Following the Yismach Yisrael, the souls of a chevra are bound together above, so learning and davening together gives strength and more kavanah.
The Mashgiach urges everyone to take on learning a mussar sefer every day, as the Chasam Sofer had his students learn Chovos HaLevavos before the shiur.

title.en: Preparing for Purim; Adar as a month of teshuvah

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer's custom of speaking before Purim, the Mashgiach explains that Purim is a renewed acceptance of the Torah and needs preparation. He brings Rav Shalom of Belz that Adar, like Elul, is a time of teshuvah, especially the second Adar, and asks for mercy for the tzaddikim and all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: What did they see, and what came upon them

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the verse 'what did they see… and what came upon them' and the Gemara's explanation of it for Achashverosh, Haman, Mordechai and Esther. He asks why Rashi follows a different version, which leaves the last question unanswered, when the Gemara seems closer to the plain meaning.

title.en: Torah with love sweetens judgments

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ohr HaChaim that Torah learned with love and awe rises to Binah, the root of judgments, and sweetens them; without such Torah, judgments are sweetened through the passing of tzaddikim. He brings the Gemara about the plague in King David's time that ended with the death of Avishai ben Tzeruyah.

title.en: Mordechai and Esther as an atonement; kiymu v'kiblu

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Mordechai refused to bow and Esther invited Haman so that their deaths would atone for the generation. The result was 'kiymu v'kiblu', Torah accepted with love, which can sweeten judgments without the tzaddikim's sacrifice, and this is why Rashi chooses this reading as the plain meaning.

title.en: Not letting go; Amalek and slackened hands

summary.en: From the Chasam Sofer the Mashgiach learns that Mordechai kept praying and fasting after the first sign of salvation, since improvement can weaken prayer while the decree still stands. He then explains Amalek's attack at Refidim as coming from the slackening of hands from Torah, and Haman, Amalek's descendant, as rising when the Jews were lax in mitzvos.

title.en: An hour of learning before Maariv

summary.en: Since the month of Adar calls for strengthening in Torah, the Mashgiach notes that the evening learning his community once had has lapsed, and proposes, without a vow, that whoever can should learn in the beis medrash for an hour before Maariv. He stresses that this is meant to strengthen diligence and the sense of responsibility, so that it becomes second nature.

title.en: The Yismach Yisrael's takanos for the beis hachasidim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Yismach Yisrael of Alexander's takanos: to learn in the beis hachasidim, since souls that stood together at Sinai come together in one chevra, and to daven there with a minyan, waiting patiently rather than being exacting. He adds the takanah against idle talk in the beis hachasidim and the measured speech of Shabbos.

title.en: A fateful time: assimilation and redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the present as a fateful time, pointing to the mass intermarriage of Jews, which he calls a destruction greater than the Holocaust about which people are silent. He compares it to Ezra's time before the Second Temple, applies Mordechai's words to Esther, 'if you are silent at this time', and says we can be Hashem's instruments for the salvation by strengthening one another.

title.en: 'Asher karcha': Amalek cools us off

summary.en: On 'asher karcha baderech' the Mashgiach says Amalek cooled them off, and asks why the fiery davening of the chevra's early years has cooled, calling for a cheshbon hanefesh. He tells a story he heard from the Satmar Rav of a tzaddik who once skipped his custom of mayim emtza'im, traced it to a conversation with a Sabbatean, and was troubled that he had become worse.

title.en: Az nidberu: the value of the chevra

summary.en: The Mashgiach says learning together at night increases friendship, and brings Malachi's last prophecy, 'then those who fear Hashem spoke to one another', for a dark time before Moshiach. He tells a story of a chassan at the Stoliner Rebbe's court who left the Rebbe's minyan, and lists the treasured parts of his own community's davening.

title.en: Yekar: feeling the preciousness; daily mussar

summary.en: Bringing the Sfas Emes on 'v'yekar', the Mashgiach says avodah was precious to the Jews then and must be precious now, not given away for money, and calls for a cheshbon hanefesh in Adar. Following the Chasam Sofer, he urges learning a mussar sefer daily, and closes with a tefillah for salvation and redemption.

catalogTitle: שמחים בפורים שלכל עומק שנופל יהודי' מכל מקום הוא חלק מה' (שייכות לפרשת זכור ותצוה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim is the Yom Tov of the 'stragglers', the Jews who fell furthest, because however low a Jew falls he remains Hashem's portion, and on Purim he should rejoice in that.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas Tetzaveh, read in the week of Zachor, where Moshe Rabbeinu's name is missing. Haman chose Adar thinking Moshe's merit had ended, but for Jews there is no 'death of Moshe': a Yehoshua always carries the Torah onward. Amalek attacked the stragglers whom the cloud had cast out of the camp, Jews the Torah calls 'not fearing G-d', and yet Hashem wages war for them. The darkness is strongest just before dawn, as in Mitzrayim, Bavel and before Moshiach. Purim came by lot, without effort, showing that every Jew is Hashem's portion; a king's child who falls into filth remains his child. The Megillah is an iggeres, a personal letter to each Jew, the more so the further he is. After stories and the Purim tefillos, the Mashgiach warns against mockery and ends with Aharon, who earned the choshen by rejoicing in his brother's greatness.

en: For the Jewish people there is no 'death of Moshe': after Moshe always comes a Yehoshua who carries the Torah further.
Even a Jew who was cast out of the camp and seems not to fear Hashem remains so dear to Him that Hashem wages war on Amalek for his sake.
The darkness is strongest at the end of every exile, just before dawn, and so it is in the time before Moshiach.
Purim came by lot, without effort, which shows what is truly one's own: every Jew is Hashem's portion, and no sin can make Him abandon His child.
Purim is the Yom Tov of the stragglers, and on it a Jew should rejoice in his point of Yiddishkeit, knowing he is a child of Hashem however far he fell.
Purim is a holy day of love and unity, not a time for mockery or for shaming another Jew.

joy in one's point of Yiddishkeit

title.en: Parshas Tetzaveh without Moshe's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Parshas Tetzaveh, read in the week of Parshas Zachor, is the parsha in which Moshe Rabbeinu's name is not mentioned. He explains that 'zachor', remembering, applies to something that tends to be forgotten.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the Jew's hope

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the end of the seventy years of the Babylonian exile, when many thought the redemption would not come and Achashverosh celebrated his calculation. He explains, with the Zohar on Vayeshev, that the nations' hatred comes from the Jew's hope, and that kings will give the Jews anything except Yerushalayim.

title.en: No 'death of Moshe' for the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman chose Adar, the month of Moshe's passing, thinking his merit had ended, but for Jews there is no death of Moshe: a Yehoshua always comes after him to carry the Torah. He ties Zachor to the danger of forgetting Torah, brings the Gemara on reviewing a hundred and one times, and notes that Parshas Zachor itself mentions Yehoshua.

title.en: The outer Jews and Yaakov's gift to Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of very simple Jews who stand as if outside the Mishkan, and says Hashem will not give up any Jew. He brings the Midrash that the animals Yaakov sent to Esav were Jewish souls, which Moshiach will reclaim, and says that even souls caught by the nachash remain bound to Moshe Rabbeinu.

title.en: Amalek and those cast out of the camp

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek attacked Hashem's honor, yet Hashem forgoes His own honor, as the Gemara about Yeravam shows. Amalek struck the stragglers whom the cloud had cast out of the camp, whom the passuk calls 'not fearing G-d', and still Hashem declares war on Amalek for their sake.

title.en: The darkest hour before dawn

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that even a Jew whom Avraham Avinu does not recognize as his child is important enough to Hashem to fight for. He explains that Adar ends the year, cloaked in nature, and that darkness grows strongest at the end of each exile: in Mitzrayim, in Bavel, and before Moshiach. Esther called out from this darkness, and Hashem did not give up even on the Jews who enjoyed Achashverosh's feast.

title.en: Purim by lot: the Jew as Hashem's portion

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the other Yamim Tovim, which need preparation, with Purim, which came by lot. A lot shows what is truly one's own without effort, and Jews are Hashem's portion. He explains that Yom Kippur is 'like Purim', that no sin can make Hashem reject a Jew, and that a king's child who falls into filth remains his child.

title.en: Purim belongs to the fallen Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the great joy of Purim is to know that one is a child of Hashem however far one has fallen, and that one who learned and davened well all year has, as it were, no special share in Purim, the day of the stragglers. Hashem tells the yetzer hara it has no right to touch a Jewish soul. He connects this to Esther's cry of Ayeles Hashachar and to matanos l'evyonim, Hashem's gifts to the poor.

title.en: The rose and Shoshanas Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that colors hint at middos, red being din and distance. A rose is red, yet even from afar its scent is sweet, and Jews remain distinguished even when far. He describes the joy of Shoshanas Yaakov, of belonging to the people that accepts malchus Shamayim, and says Purim reveals Hashem's 'rav chesed', whose color is white.

title.en: The Megillah as a sefer and an iggeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the Megillah is called both a sefer and an iggeres, and explains the difference: a book is for whoever wants it, while a letter is addressed to one person. A Jew may feel a sefer Torah is not for him, but no one refuses a letter from the king with his own name on it; the Megillah is such a letter to every Jew, the more so the further he is.

title.en: Purim's letters to every Jew and the avodah of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim that on Purim one can ask for everything, but one needs sense, and tells of a man whose blessings were all fulfilled until Heaven made him a drunkard. Purim is made for the drunk and the stragglers; the King sends His letters to every province. He explains that the preparation for Pesach begins on Purim, and that the avodah of Purim is not a day of mikveh and Tehillim but rejoicing as a fallen Jew in one's point of Yiddishkeit.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam and the broken dam

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story brought in seforim of Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam: when a dam broke on Purim, the queen sent for his tefillah, and he responded by drinking, dancing and rejoicing, and the danger passed. He explains that the Jews' will counts in Heaven because they do Hashem's will, and on Purim Hashem's will is feasting and joy.

title.en: Taanis Esther's tefillah and the light revealed on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one must come before the King like Esther, and that on Taanis Esther one should find time to say the kapitel of Ayeles Hashachar. He reads from a sefer of one of the early mekubalim that a hidden world created in the days of Mordechai and Esther is revealed with the reading of the Megillah, a light of 'rav chesed' that Shabbos reveals only for a moment. Because this holiness is so great, he explains, it can only be received through drinking.

title.en: Not a day for mockery; Yom Kippur and Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that Purim is a holy day of forgiveness and unity, not a time for foolishness, mockery or insulting others and the honor of Torah, which the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah never intended. He reads the end of Parshas Tetzaveh, where 'once a year' appears twice, as hinting at two atonements: the avodah of Yom Kippur and the 'avodah without avodah' of Purim, a Yom Tov for the stragglers.

title.en: Aharon's choshen: joy in another's greatness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Aharon merited the choshen on his heart because he rejoiced in the greatness of his younger brother Moshe. Purim is a time of love, without envy or shaming, when each Jew rejoices in his own point. A leader of Klal Yisrael, like Moshe who went from the mountain straight to the people and Aharon who carried their judgment on his heart, must not have himself in mind. He closes with a vort of Rabbi Mordechai of Lechovitch on joy that makes the soul shine.

catalogTitle: The Avodah of the Day - Connect Yourself to the Essence of Your נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur is the fortieth, innermost level of the Jewish soul, the yechidah, where every Jew truly wants to serve Hashem and all Jews are one, and from this he explains why appeasing others, malkus and mikveh on Erev Yom Kippur share one siman in the Shulchan Aruch.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Shulchan Aruch puts three Erev Yom Kippur practices in one siman: appeasing anyone one has wronged, receiving malkus, and immersing in the mikveh. He brings the Noam Elimelech on an upper world of Klal Yisrael, the level of yechidah where all souls are fused as one and no blemish reaches. He then brings the Ramban that the forty lashes match the forty stages of a child's formation, asks why only thirty-nine are given, and answers with the Rambam on compelled consent: the innermost fortieth level never sinned. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul form the year, and Yom Kippur, the fortieth, is when the yechidah surfaces. Yom Kippur is also the mikveh of Klal Yisrael. He ends with the Midrash of the tailor who paid twelve dinarim for a fish, showing love of Hashem that brings forgiveness.

en: Appeasing others, malkus and tevilah on Erev Yom Kippur appear together in one siman of the Shulchan Aruch, so there must be a link between them.
According to the Mashgiach, the innermost level of the soul, the yechidah, is where all Jews are fused into one soul and where no sin reaches.
Only thirty-nine lashes are given because the fortieth, innermost stage of a person was never blemished by the sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur form the coming year, and Yom Kippur is the fortieth day, when the yechidah comes to the surface.
Yom Kippur is the mikveh of Klal Yisrael, the fortieth se'ah, so any quarrel left unresolved is a chatzitzah between one Jew and another.
The tailor who paid twelve dinarim for a fish showed his love of Hashem, and that love is itself the proof that he will be forgiven.

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that siman 606 of the Shulchan Aruch joins appeasing those one has wronged, malkus and tevilah, and asks what links them. He brings the Noam Elimelech on an upper world of Klal Yisrael where all souls are fused as one and no blemish reaches.

title.en: Forty lashes and the untouched fortieth level

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that the forty lashes correspond to the forty stages of a child's formation, and asks why only thirty-nine are given. He answers with the Rambam on coercing someone until he says 'I want': deep down every Jew wants to serve Hashem, so the innermost fortieth stage was never blemished.

title.en: Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, and the yechidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul form the year like the forty days of a child's formation, and Yom Kippur is the fortieth, when the soul's cry of 'I want' surfaces. He recalls a Rebbe teaching the five parts of the soul and says the aim of Yom Kippur is to consciously meet one's yechidah, which is also why it is a day of unity and of appeasing others.

title.en: Yom Kippur as the mikveh of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the end of Mishnah Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem', and explains that each day of the forty adds a se'ah until Yom Kippur completes the mikveh. This explains the Kohen Gadol's immersions and our tevilah on Erev Yom Kippur, and ties all three practices of the siman to unity, since a quarrel is a chatzitzah.

title.en: The Midrash of the tailor and the fish

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash brought by the Tur: a Jewish tailor outbid the governor's servant and paid twelve dinarim for the only fish on Erev Yom Kippur. Summoned by the governor, he explained that Jews rejoice with fine food on Erev Yom Kippur, and the governor let him go.

title.en: Love of Hashem as the proof of forgiveness

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Midrash stresses the price and calls the tailor's words a proof. Comparing it to paying a high price for an esrog, he explains that spending beyond worth expresses love of Hashem, and since Hashem returns love, it proves He will forgive. He closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov's three loves and a call for love of Torah and of Jews in a year he expects to be momentous.

catalogTitle: נתגלה עולם חדש של “יחידה”

oneLiner.en: Reading from the Yesod Yosef, the Mashgiach explains that the miracle of Purim created a new, awesome world above, the root of Mordechai's soul and the world of yechidah where all Jewish souls become one, and that on Purim this light comes down to this world for those who are united with all Jews.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with practical words for those traveling to Yerushalayim for Purim Meshulash: rest before the reading, hear the Megillah together with the public, and if a word is missed say it at once and catch up. He stresses that Purim is a serious, holy day and introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef with a story of the Beis Aharon. The Yesod Yosef says the miracle of Mordechai and Esther created a new holy world above, the root of Mordechai's soul, which is not revealed outward. The Mashgiach ties it to Yom Kippur, called 'like Purim': both reach the world of yechidah, where all souls become one, and only through unity. On Yom Kippur we rise to it; on Purim it comes down. He discusses drinking on Purim, the special wine and tzedakah of the day, the blessing on the Megillah as a call to its light, the fully opened Megillah, and the ever-growing joy of Adar.

en: According to the Yesod Yosef, the miracle of Mordechai and Esther created a new, holy and awesome world above that had never existed before, and it is not revealed outward.
That world is the root of Mordechai's soul and is the world of yechidah, the level at which all Jewish souls merge into one soul.
Yom Kippur reaches the same world, but on Yom Kippur Jews rise up to it like angels, while on Purim the light comes down into this world, sanctifying even the body.
Just as one has no Yom Kippur without unity and forgiving one another, one cannot receive the light of Purim without achdus with all Jews.
The blessing 'al mikra Megillah' means calling the Megillah, calling its hidden light down, so it should be said and heard with trembling and with the intent to become a vessel for that light.
'When Adar enters, joy increases' means that joy must keep growing day by day through the month, just as from Rosh Chodesh Av the sadness keeps deepening until Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Preparing for Purim in Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions his trip to Yerushalayim for Purim Meshulash and the jet lag he once felt at the Megillah reading. He advises travelers to rest beforehand, to hear the Megillah together with the public, and explains what to do if a word is missed.

title.en: Purim as a holy day; the Yesod Yosef

summary.en: Citing the Chasam Sofer on speaking about Purim beforehand, the Mashgiach stresses that Purim is a serious, holy day, greater than Yom Kippur. He introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef and tells how the Beis Aharon praised a simple Jew who loved the words of Shir HaShirim without understanding them.

title.en: A new world: the root of Mordechai's soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Yesod Yosef: Purim brought a new holy world into being, the root of Mordechai's soul, which is not revealed outward. He links it to Yom Kippur, 'like Purim', and explains that both are the world of yechidah, reached only through unity: on Yom Kippur we rise to it, on Purim it comes down.

title.en: How to drink on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach sharply criticizes disgraceful drunkenness on Purim and contrasts it with the Satmar Rav, who drank and revealed secrets of the Torah. He describes how the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov drank a little and napped, and how Rabbi Avraham of Ciechanow drank a measured revi'is of wine.

title.en: The wine and tzedakah of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the wine and the matanos l'evyonim of Purim are of a different kind, as an esrog becomes precious on Sukkos. He returns to the difference between Yom Kippur and Purim, saying the light comes down to this world on Purim, that one must pray for it, and that it requires achdus.

title.en: Unity against Haman, and calling the Megillah

summary.en: Against Haman's 'scattered and divided' and Amalek at Refidim, Purim is unity, expressed in mishloach manos joining all tables into one. The Mashgiach says one must pray to merit the light, cites the Arizal, and explains that 'al mikra Megillah' means calling the hidden light of the Megillah down to us.

title.en: Kavanah at the blessing; the open Megillah

summary.en: Continuing the Yesod Yosef, the Mashgiach explains that the one reading should say the blessing with trembling and that each listener should intend to become a vessel for the light now revealed. He then explains why the Megillah is opened fully and folded like a letter rather than rolled like a Sefer Torah: the hidden is revealed.

title.en: Joy that keeps growing in Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach recommends a kuntres of sources on Purim and answers a question he was asked at a sheva brachos: 'when Adar enters, joy increases' means joy grows greater every day, just as the mourning of Av deepens step by step until Tisha B'Av. He closes with a blessing for a joyous month and a bright Purim.

catalogTitle: יו"ט שמלמד איך לשחוק על העולם

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim, the day of Adar when miracles are cloaked in nature and Hashem's name is hidden, teaches a Jew to read the Megillah, history and his own life until he sees that Hashem pulls every string, and to laugh at the world's puppet show.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Chasam Sofer: Purim is not a day of foolishness but a day whose light exceeds even the Torah of Moshe, and the Rabbonim used to speak before it to awaken teshuvah. He contrasts Nissan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, whose name comes from aderes, a cloak: the Purim miracles are wrapped in nature, and the Megillah never mentions Hashem's name. The Bnei Yissaschar's parable of the sick man and the 'coincidences' of the Megillah show that a hidden miracle is greater than the splitting of the sea. The concealment is Amalek's work, the klipah of chance and doubt; yet 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem, and His name hides in its initials. With the parable of a puppet show, the Rashash's watch and a doctor reading an X-ray, the Mashgiach teaches that a Jew must learn to read the Megillah, the newspaper and his own day this way. He closes with the Yesod Yosef on the great light revealed at the Megillah reading, and asks that Purim be prepared for and kept seriously.

en: Purim is a very great day; the Chasam Sofer and the Kedushas Levi say the light of the Megillah is even greater than that of the Torah of Moshe.
Nissan is the month of open miracles that change nature; Adar, from aderes (a cloak), is the month of miracles wrapped in nature, and so the Megillah never mentions Hashem's name.
The concealment of Hashem is the klipah of Amalek, which makes a Jew say everything 'just happened' and casts doubt into his heart.
The whole world is Hashem's puppet show: kings and presidents only move because He pulls the strings, and one who knows this can look at the world and laugh.
Hashem's name is in fact everywhere in the Megillah, hidden in initials and between the words, and a Jew must learn to read the Megillah the way a doctor learns to read an X-ray.
The lesson of Purim is to see Hashem guiding history, current events and everything that happens to a person from Modeh Ani until he goes to sleep, and to carry this through the whole year.
At the Megillah reading a great light from a 'new world' is revealed, and a Jew must prepare himself through teshuvah to be a vessel to receive it.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: Purim is a great day

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that people mistake Purim for a day of foolishness, while the light of the Megillah is greater than that of the Torah of Moshe, as the Kedushas Levi also says. Therefore the Rabbonim used to speak before Purim to stir the people to teshuvah.

title.en: From Nissan to Adar: miracles seen and unseen

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the months descend from Nissan, the month of open miracles, to Adar, the lowest. A nes is a banner raised for all to see, but a plain reading of the Megillah shows only a palace story without a single miracle or mention of Hashem; only a believing Jew sees the miracles there.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar's parable of the sick man

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man whose only cure and only doctor are across the sea, and both arrive by ship that very day. He applies it to the chain of 'just then' events in the Megillah and concludes that a miracle within nature is no smaller than the splitting of the sea, and even greater.

title.en: Adar as aderes, and the Adar of history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar comes from aderes, a cloak: its miracles are veiled in nature. Our generation, at the heels of Moshiach, lives in the Adar of history, with hidden miracles like the fall of Russia and the threat from Iraq; the Megillah too came at the end of the Babylonian exile. He brings the Midrash that 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem.

title.en: Amalek covers Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem's name is missing if 'the King' means Him, and answers that the klipah of Amalek covers it: the Name and the Throne are incomplete while Amalek exists, Amalek 'happened upon you' and calls everything chance, and Amalek equals safek, doubt. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that hamelech, kes and Haman all equal 95.

title.en: The puppet show: laughing at the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a puppet show whose wooden figures dance only because experts above pull thin strings, and applies it to world leaders such as Bush and Saddam Hussein: Hashem moves them all. One who knows this can sit back, look at the world and laugh. The plain meaning of 'the King' is Achashverosh, the derash is Hashem, and the two do not contradict.

title.en: Hashem's name hidden between the words

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah, as in the initials of 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom', which a chassidish ba'al koreh reads in one breath. Hashem watches through the cracks, as in 'mashgiach min hachalonos', and the Megillah reflects hester panim; one must learn to read it and to see Hashem's hand in every timely event.

title.en: The Rashash and the soldier's watch

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter visited the Rashash in Vilna when the Rashash's watch had broken; the Rashash trusted that Hashem would send him one, and a Jewish soldier arrived with a gold watch a dying comrade had asked him to give to a talmid chacham. The Mashgiach calls it hashgachah pratis and says the more a Jew trusts, the more he sees it.

title.en: Reading the Megillah like an X-ray

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the Megillah to an X-ray: a layman sees only black and white, while a trained doctor reads it. No book of Tanach has as many commentaries, and every verse is a gear in the clock that brings the miracle. Reading it this way one can say the brachah She'asah Nissim, and learn to see Hashem in the newspaper, in history and in each day of one's life.

title.en: The Jewish people a miracle; Adar and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kuzari that the survival of the Jewish people through every exile and every Haman shows Hashem plainly. He then speaks of the holiness of Purim and Adar, Adar Sheni in particular, of Purim's link to Yom Kippur through the goral, of Hashem preparing the cure at the very moment of the sin, and of the Rebbe of Belz on doing teshuvah in Adar.

title.en: Hashem comes down on Purim; Purim salvations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the greatness of the Megillah is that holiness enters nature: on Yom Kippur we rise to Hashem, on Purim Hashem comes down to our lowest levels. Purim is a day of salvation for which one prepares with the teshuvah of Taanis Esther, and he recalls Stalin's end on Purim and the Scud missiles of the Gulf War, which ended on Purim.

title.en: The Megillah happens every year

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled the mitzvah, read as reading it as an old story: the Megillah happens every year. He describes Achashverosh, who hated Jews and the Beis Hamikdash and made his feast over a miscalculation of the seventy years, yet was forced to do good for the Jews; tzaddikim know how to read the Megillah and draw down such salvations.

title.en: The brachos of the Megillah; Esther's psalm

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the brachah 'al mikra megillah' through the Kozhnitzer Maggid: Megillas Esther means revealing what is hidden. The brachah after the Megillah is a combined brachah because all salvations are contained in it. He brings the Yesod Yosef that saying Tehillim 22, which Esther said, with kavanah on Taanis Esther is a segulah for salvation, and describes the great holiness at the Megillah reading.

title.en: The main Purim is by day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the main Megillah reading and the mitzvos of Purim are by day, and criticizes those who carouse all night, sleep through davening and doze through the Megillah. He says one should rise with a clear head, give matanos la'evyonim and mishloach manos, daven with kavanah and hear every word of the Megillah, serving with joy and closeness to Hashem.

title.en: Yesod Yosef: the new world revealed at the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the Yesod Yosef, praised in a haskamah of Rabbi Aharon of Chernobyl: the light of Purim, like the light of Kedushah on Shabbos, comes from a 'new world' that descends once a year at the Megillah reading. The brachah 'al mikra megillah' calls it down, to be said with awe, and each Jew must prepare to be a vessel; he closes that Purim is no joke but a day of great salvation.

catalogTitle: צריכים לחפש הקב"ה שהטמין עצמו בהמגילה ובעולם הטבע

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that Hashem hid Himself in the Megillah and in the world of nature, His Name concealed in the first and last letters of its words, and that a Jew must search for Him until he finds Him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with this year's special Purim, when Yerushalayim has three days of Purim. On Purim, he says, holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written openly in the Megillah; the Midrash reads 'the King' as Hashem, and the miracles are clothed in nature. He then explains how the Name is hidden in the first or last letters of words: in order it signals the attribute of kindness, reversed it signals judgment. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the permutation of each month, and shows the Name in several verses of the Megillah, matching the Gemara's two blessings after the reading. With the story of Reb Baruch'l and the hidden child, he says Hashem hides and waits to be sought, and that the world, like the Megillah, is full of hidden miracles. He closes with the Maharal on the fifteenth of Adar, the full moon, and Shushan Purim falling on Shabbos, when the Megillah 'reads itself'.

en: On Purim holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written openly in the Megillah; He is hidden in the word 'the King' and in miracles clothed in nature.
The Name hidden in the initial letters of words in order expresses kindness; reversed, or in the final letters, it expresses judgment.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, each month has its own permutation of the Name, and the month's character matches it, as with Nissan and Tammuz.
Hashem hides in the Megillah and in the world, and He waits for Jews to search for Him.
One who knows how to read the Megillah can read the world: the whole world is a greater Megillah full of hidden miracles for the sake of the Jewish people.
When Shushan Purim falls on Shabbos in Yerushalayim, the Megillah is not read, and the Mashgiach says it is as if Hashem Himself reads it, and one must prepare to hear it.

title.en: Why Hashem's Name is hidden in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions this year's special Purim and that in Yerushalayim Purim lasts several days. He explains that on Purim holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written in the Megillah, brings the Midrash that 'the King' there means Hashem, and says the Megillah's miracles are clothed in nature, which makes them greater.

title.en: The Name in order and reversed; the months

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets out the rule: Hashem's Name in the initial letters of words, in order, is kindness; reversed or in the final letters it is judgment, since the yud gives and the heh receives. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its permutation of the Name, and shows how Nissan's pleasant spring and Tammuz's harsh heat match theirs.

title.en: The Name in the Megillah's verses

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows Hashem's Name in verses of the Megillah: in order when Esther invites the king and Haman, reversed when Haman says 'all this is worth nothing to me', and in the final letters at the climax, when Haman's downfall was decided. He ties this to the Gemara's two blessings after the Megillah, for the downfall of the enemy and for the salvation of the Jews, and concludes that one must search the Megillah for where Hashem hides, as the Gemara finds Esther in 'I will surely hide My face'.

title.en: Reb Baruch'l's tears and today's hidden miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how a child cried to Reb Baruch'l that he hid and nobody looked for him, and Reb Baruch'l wept that Hashem says the same. He then describes the daily miracles in Eretz Yisrael and in each Jew's life, which people do not notice, and the verses about Hashem's eyes resting on the land and on Yerushalayim.

title.en: The world as a greater Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah's miracles happened within nature, a chain of events over nine years that could not happen by chance, and brings the Gemara that Memuchan was Haman, whose own advice led to his downfall. Whoever knows how to read the Megillah can read the news: the world is a greater Megillah, its leaders disguised players, and an honest Jew finds Hashem in everything, peering through the cracks.

title.en: The fifteenth of Adar, Yerushalayim and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to this year's three-day Purim in Yerushalayim. He brings the Maharal that Esther asked for another day in Shushan so that somewhere Purim would fall on the fifteenth, when the moon is full, and links Yerushalayim to the moon. Since Shushan Purim falls on Shabbos and the Megillah is not read, he says Hashem Himself reads it, noting that the Mishnah says the Megillah 'is read', and urges preparing spiritual ears; he closes that Purim is a time for great salvations.

catalogTitle: Asking Forgiveness ערב יו”כ - A Deeper Understanding

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur, the fortieth day from Rosh Chodesh Elul, reaches the untouched innermost point of every Jew where all of Klal Yisrael is one, which is why appeasing one's fellow and receiving only thirty-nine lashes belong to Erev Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shulchan Aruch siman 606, which holds three halachos for Erev Yom Kippur yet is captioned only for appeasing one's fellow. He recalls Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz's one talk in the beis medrash about Yechida, the level where all souls merge as Knesses Yisrael, and the call to meet it on Yom Kippur. Through the Rambam on coerced consent and the Ohr HaChaim on Korach he shows that the point of Yaakov Avinu in every Jew stays unblemished. The Ramban ties forty lashes to the forty days of a fetus's formation; only thirty-nine are given because the first point is never damaged. He applies this to Adam's thirty-nine curses, the thirty-nine melachos and Yosef, who saw his father's image. Yom Kippur is the fortieth day of the year's formation, a day of unity and a mikveh, sealed at Ne'ilah.

en: Yechida, the highest level of the soul, is where all Jewish souls merge into the one soul of Knesses Yisrael, and on Yom Kippur a Jew can make contact with it.
Deep in every Jew's heart is a point drawn from Yaakov Avinu that wants only the will of Hashem and that no sin can blemish.
A transgression blemishes thirty-nine of the forty stages of a person's formation, but not the first point where Hashem began creating him, so the Torah gives only thirty-nine lashes.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation of the year, and Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, is where a Jew touches Yechida and the oneness of Knesses Yisrael.
Because Yom Kippur is a day of unity, one cannot enter it while in conflict with another Jew, which is why appeasing one's fellow belongs to Erev Yom Kippur.
Yom Kippur is itself a mikveh, filled through the teshuvah of the forty days, and its climax is the sealing of Ne'ilah.
