title.en: Siman 606 and Rav Shraga Feivel's talk

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Shulchan Aruch siman 606 contains three halachos, appeasing one's fellow, receiving lashes and a third, yet its caption names only appeasing, and asks why. He then recalls how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz once interrupted the learning to speak about Yechida and urged the bochurim to find the moment on Yom Kippur when they touch it and build their year on it.

title.en: The untouched point of Yaakov Avinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Yechida as the collective soul of Knesses Yisrael and brings the Rambam that coerced consent counts, because deep down every Jew wants Hashem's will. He traces this inner point to Yaakov Avinu, the trunk of the tree, and brings the Ohr HaChaim that Korach is not called a son of Yisrael because his blemish reached his fathers but not Yaakov.

title.en: Forty lashes and thirty-nine

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that lashes number forty because a sinner damages the forty days of his formation, and asks why only thirty-nine are given. He answers that the first point, where Hashem began creating the person, is never blemished: it is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the heart, the hidden love of the Tanya, untouched even in the worst Jew, and likewise Adam's sin brought thirty-nine curses but not a fortieth.

title.en: Yosef, the fortieth day and unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's count of thirty-nine or forty mentions of melachah, depending on Yosef's 'melachto', and explains that Yosef, near breaking, saw the image of Yaakov Avinu, the point that cannot be destroyed. He then counts forty days of formation from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day when a Jew touches Yechida and Knesses Yisrael, and concludes that one must be reconciled with every Jew to enter it.

title.en: Why these halachos share one siman

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to siman 606: lashes are received on Erev Yom Kippur, the thirty-ninth day, and never forty, because the fortieth day is Yom Kippur where no sin reaches. Citing Rav Yaakov Emden that the Shulchan Aruch was written with ruach hakodesh, he explains why appeasing and the thirty-nine lashes belong together, and adds the immersion of Erev Yom Kippur, since Yom Kippur itself is a mikveh.

title.en: The mikveh of Yom Kippur and Ne'ilah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the forty days of Elul as pouring forty se'ah of teshuvah into the mikveh of Yom Kippur, the day the pure point surfaces in every Jew. Like the Kohen Gadol, every Jew enters the Kodesh HaKodashim of his own heart, and at Ne'ilah each one re-enacts the tribes' declaration at Yaakov Avinu's bedside, a seal that remains all year. He closes with blessings for the coming year.

catalogTitle: שמחת אדר ע"י "פקודי ה' ישרים משמחי לב"

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the simcha of Adar comes to a Jew through "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev": the joy of learning with clarity, of davening well and of giving tzedakah, after first explaining why a Jew should be content to serve Hashem where He has placed him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with "mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha" and with the many people traveling to Eretz Yisroel for Purim. Purim was created in galus, he says, and a Jew should be content where he is: great tzaddikim such as the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim wanted to go and were held back from Heaven. Galus is a shlichus to raise sparks of holiness, and one must know where a desire to travel comes from. Turning to Adar, he contrasts the goy's joy from a bottle with the Jew's joy from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev". Learning a blatt Gemara until it becomes clear brings great simcha; Adar, when the Torah was accepted anew after prophecy ended, is the time of Torah she'be'al peh. Simcha is the sign of good learning and good davening, which feed each other, and tzedakah given beyond one's means also brings simcha. He closes with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah as the joy of Purim, and a brachah.

en: A goy seeks happiness in a bottle and ends up more depressed, while a Jew's simcha comes from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev": doing Hashem's will through learning and davening.
When a blatt Gemara becomes clear and new understanding opens up, it brings tremendous simcha, and the clearer it becomes the greater the joy.
Adar is the time of Torah she'be'al peh: after prophecy ended with the first Beis HaMikdash, the miracle of Purim brought a new acceptance of the Torah with love and joy.
Simcha is the sign of proper learning and proper davening, and the two feed each other: Torah is of the mind and tefillah of the heart, and a person needs both.
Giving tzedakah beyond one's means brings simcha afterwards, and Torah, tefillah and tzedakah together are part of the joy of Purim.
A Jew should be content where Hashem has placed him: galus is a shlichus, and the circumstances that keep a person where he is show that this is what Hashem wants.

candidateTopics: Purim in galus and in Eretz Yisroel
Torah she'be'al peh and ruach hakodesh

title.en: Purim in Eretz Yisroel or in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the simcha of Adar and the many who travel to Eretz Yisroel for Purim. He says Purim was created in galus, that Purim in a walled city belongs to higher levels, and that a Jew must be content where he is, bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim, who wanted to go and were held back from Heaven.

title.en: Galus as a shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem sent the Jews into galus to gather "converts", which the Arizal reads as sparks of holiness, and compares every Jew's home to a shliach's Chabad house. One must know where the desire to travel stems from, not imitate others, and if the means are lacking, Hashem is telling him to stay.

title.en: Contentment with Hashem's plan

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of shluchim sent back from 770 and says each person must make an honest reckoning, never borrow money for such a trip or burden his parents. He describes the level of wanting nothing but what Hashem wants, notes that the Talmud Bavli and the great works of Torah came about in galus, and says no one knows Hashem's plans in what is happening now in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev

summary.en: Turning to his topic, the Mashgiach asks how one increases simcha in Adar. He contrasts the goy who drinks to become happy and wakes up depressed with the Jew whose joy comes from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev", and describes the tremendous simcha of a blatt Gemara that becomes clear.

title.en: Adar, Torah she'be'al peh and ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that learning is a wondrous union with Hashem, and that Adar is the time of Torah she'be'al peh: after prophecy ended, the Torah was accepted anew with love at Purim, and ruach hakodesh now means arriving at the truth in the Gemara. The test of whether one learned properly is simcha.

title.en: Tefillah, learning and deveikus

summary.en: The Mashgiach says learning needs siyata dishmaya and therefore tefillah, brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that the sign of good davening is simcha afterwards, and explains that Torah (mind) and tefillah (heart) bring each other. Deveikus is for everyone at his level, as he shows from the Sanzer Rav and Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz.

title.en: Good davening and the joy of tzedakah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that with Hashem's help there is good davening in the beis medrash, and one who does not take advantage of it is wasteful, especially in Adar. He describes the simcha felt after giving tzedakah beyond one's means, brings "pasoach tiftach" and the teaching that tzedakah is central in the time before Moshiach, and concludes that Torah, tefillah and tzedakah are part of the simcha of Purim.

title.en: Matanos la'evyonim and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that matanos la'evyonim are meant to gladden the hearts of the poor, says Adar is a time of Torah, tzedakah and tefillah when prayers are accepted, and blesses all to merit the full simcha of the redemption. The end turns to the festive gathering with cake and wine.

title.en: Closing

summary.en: Closing.

catalogTitle: מעלת השנה שחל בו פורים המשולש

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why a year of Purim Meshulash, when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, is a rare time ripe for geulah, and calls on the lowest generation to bring Moshiach through Torah, tefillah and a clean mouth.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens after Chanukah: Purim belongs to Moshiach ben Yosef and Nissan to Moshiach ben David, and Adar prepares for Nissan. This year is rare: the Imrei Noam, citing the Rimanover, writes that the final geulah will come in a year when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos. He links Purim Meshulash to Yosef revealing himself to his brothers. He then explains 'velo ya'avor': Purim cannot pass the fifteenth, since from the sixteenth the waning moon is the domain of Eisav and Amalek, which cannot be entered before Moshiach; only in Purim Meshulash is the seudah held on the sixteenth. Why did such years pass without Moshiach? There was a hole in the pocket. Yet our generation, facing unprecedented trials, is asked for less and can bring Moshiach. He urges hasmadah, kavanah and guarding the mouth, warns against pressuring fathers to pay for Purim trips, and closes that the lowest generation's task is to bring Moshiach.

en: A year of Purim Meshulash is always a year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, a kevius the Imrei Noam, citing the Rimanover, ties to the final geulah.
Purim may not be held after the fifteenth ('velo ya'avor') because from the sixteenth, as the moon wanes, is the domain of Eisav and Amalek, which cannot be entered until Moshiach comes.
In Purim Meshulash the seudah in Yerushalayim falls on Sunday, the sixteenth, so once in decades the Jews do enter Eisav's domain.
Earlier generations had such years and Moshiach did not come, because there was a 'hole in the pocket' through which the merit fell out.
Our generation faces trials earlier generations never had, so only a little is asked of it, and its small efforts give great nachas ruach.
The Mashgiach calls for learning with hasmadah, davening with kavanah and guarding the mouth, so that the Torah and tefillah that pass through it are pure.
Every generation has its task, and the task of the lowest generation, the 'heel' of the generations, is to bring Moshiach.

candidateTopics: velo ya'avor and the waning moon

title.en: A rare year: Erev Pesach on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Purim is Moshiach ben Yosef and Nissan Moshiach ben David, with Adar preparing for Nissan. He reads the Imrei Noam, who brings from the Rimanover that the final geulah will come in a year when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, as this year does.

title.en: Yosef's revelation and the waning moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties Purim Meshulash to Yosef's 'Ani Yosef', a sign that Hashem will reveal that the whole galus was for the good. He then asks why Purim may not pass the fifteenth, and explains that from the sixteenth the moon wanes and the sitra achra, whose head is the angel of Eisav, rules, as shown by the Shulchan Aruch's limit on weddings.

title.en: Entering Eisav's domain on Purim Meshulash

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Edom's refusal, 'lo sa'avor bi', and explains the Gemara's 'velo ya'avor': before Moshiach one cannot enter Eisav's domain on the sixteenth. Only in Purim Meshulash, when the seudah in Yerushalayim is on Sunday the sixteenth, does one cross over, and such a year always has Erev Pesach on Shabbos.

title.en: A hole in the pocket; Hillel becomes Nasi

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why such years came before without Moshiach, and answers with the havdalah segulah for sons and the 'hole in the pocket'. He brings that Hillel became Nasi through a Shabbos Erev Pesach, a nesius from Beis Dovid that is a sign of Moshiach, and says the generations keep growing smaller.

title.en: Why Moshiach can come in our weak generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings R' Chezkel of Kuzmir's statement that Moshiach would come in his time, which drew laughter since he had not come in the days of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the great tzaddikim. He answers that less is expected of later generations, whose trials, such as kavanah in tefillah and guarding the eyes, are far harder, so a little gives great nachas ruach.

title.en: Mending the pocket: Torah, tefillah, a clean mouth

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings R' Avraham of Slonim that Jews must be told how strong they are, and says this year may be the time of Moshiach if the pockets are mended. He calls for hasmadah, kavanah and guarding the mouth from lashon hara, since Torah and tefillah pass through the mouth, and turns to the bochurim's plans to travel for Purim Meshulash, warning against a mitzvah haba'ah ba'aveirah.

title.en: Purim trips, the rabbanim and tzedakah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says fathers in his shul of poor kollel yungeleit and melamdim must not be pressed to pay for a trip to Eretz Yisrael, since Mordechai himself kept Purim outside Yerushalayim, and one should do what the rabbanim say. He discusses the rabbanim's plan for the busy Friday and a Sunday gathering for tzedakah, and the Shulchan Aruch on when a Chanukah meal is a seudas mitzvah.

title.en: The lowest generation's task

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Yosef's five garments to Binyamin hint at Mordechai's five royal garments, and urges using the three months until Erev Pesach for learning and tefillos. He asks each person to make a cheshbon hanefesh about why he was sent into the world now, and answers that the lowest generation, the 'heel', is meant to bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: זמן שאפילו שוכחי ה' ישובו (שייכות לז' אדר ולפ' ויקרא)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the month of Adar, bound up with Moshe Rabbeinu's humility and his Mishkan, is the time when even the Jews who have forgotten Hashem are called back with love, and that Purim draws down hidden chassadim on Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the custom of recalling Moshe Rabbeinu's merit in Adar and with the idea of 'borrowing' from a better future, illustrated by a story of a Kotzker chassid. From the small alef of Vayikra he explains Moshe's humility and how every Jew who shares it is called closer, even in the hiddenness of Adar, when Hashem's name is missing from the Megillah. He then ties Adar, and especially Adar Sheni, to the forgotten Jews outside the camp: the extra silver of the shekalim that Moshe forgot became the hooks of the pillars, which stood outside the courtyard and will yet be joined back. Moshe's Mishkan, he says, was never truly destroyed; every Mikdash is a copy of it, and its holiness still shields Klal Yisrael. He speaks of Amalek in place, soul and time, reads from Yesod Yosef about Taanis Esther and the light revealed at the Megillah reading, and ends with the Name of Hashem hidden in the Megillah, showing that Purim is chessed for Israel and din for its enemies.

en: The Mashgiach says that one who accepts upon himself in Adar to keep and learn Torah, 'kiyemu v'kiblu', gains a connection to Moshe Rabbeinu, whose soul is spread through every Jew.
Moshe wrote Vayikra with a small alef because he held himself smaller than everyone; a Jew who takes on that humility is called in by Hashem with a call of love.
Adar, and especially Adar Sheni, is the time of those outside the camp who have forgotten Hashem, and Purim is when they are brought back in.
Every Mikdash and every sanctuary a Jew builds for Hashem is a copy of the Mishkan Moshe made, and its holiness still protects Klal Yisrael.
Adar is the time of Amalek in the year, and the mitzvos of Purim are what equip Jews to wage war against him.
Hashem's Name is hidden in the Megillah in a form that brings chassadim to Israel and judgment to its enemies, and every year the same kindness returns.

Mishkan of Moshe and the Batei Mikdash
Amalek in place, soul and time
Hashem's name hidden in the Megillah

title.en: Moshe's merit and borrowing from the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the custom of recalling Moshe Rabbeinu's merit and the teaching that the final redemption will come in his merit, through Torah. Since Jews are not yet fully devoted to Torah, he explains that they 'borrow' from the future, as in the Kotzk story of a chassid who called Hashem 'Father', and as in the 'kiyemu v'kiblu' of Purim.

title.en: The small alef of Vayikra

summary.en: From this week's parsha the Mashgiach explains Moshe's reluctance to enter the Ohel Moed and the small alef of Vayikra, citing the Baal HaTurim and Rashi, and the Midrash that the leftover ink gave Moshe his radiant face. He adds that Moshe is the inclusive soul of all Israel, present in every Jew.

title.en: Called close even in hiddenness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that through Moshe's humility a Jew is called in with love, even in the hiddenness of Adar, when Hashem's name is absent both in 'vayikra el Moshe' and in the Megillah. A large alef is seen from afar, a small one only from close; the Megillah is Mordechai's message to the distant, and on Purim even those who forgot Hashem return.

title.en: Pekudei, Adar Sheni and the forgotten silver

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Moshe's name is missing in Tetzaveh but appears thirteen times in Pekudei, and ties this to a leap year's second hiddenness and greater revelation. He calls Adar the time of those outside the camp, and brings the Midrash that Moshe forgot what he did with the 1,775 extra shekels until he remembered they became hooks for the pillars.

title.en: The hooks outside the courtyard

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six hundred thousand whose shekalim made the silver sockets are the core of the camp, while the extra Jews are the forgotten ones, connected to the forgetting of Torah that Osniel ben Kenaz restored through pilpul. The hooks stood outside the courtyard, yet will be joined back to the pillars, since every Jew is a 'head' in some way.

title.en: Every Mikdash is Moshe's Mishkan

summary.en: On 'eileh pekudei haMishkan, Mishkan ha'Eidus' the Mashgiach brings Rashi's reading of the double word as a pledge for the two destructions, and the Yismach Moshe's answer that every Mikdash is really the Mishkan Moshe made. He illustrates with a poet's original manuscript and its copies.

title.en: The diamond that saved a life

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Moshe's Mishkan could be lost when the Gemara says Moshe's handiwork cannot be destroyed, and answers with the mashal of a son who gave his father's diamond to save his life. Moshe's holiness absorbed the wrath meant for Israel, and Mordechai, a spark of Moshe, likewise saved the Jews.

title.en: Amalek in soul and in time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek exists in soul, in souls that spread heresy and doubt in emunah, especially before Moshiach, and in time, at the end of the year farthest from Nisan. Just as the mitzvah of wiping out Amalek applies to a known Amalekite, so in Adar one must wage war with Amalek, and the mitzvos of Purim equip Jews for it.

title.en: Yesod Yosef on Taanis Esther

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef and reads from it that on Taanis Esther Mordechai and Esther come down to join the Jews. Mordechai saw the inner root of Haman's power, and Esther stood in the inner courtyard above; the scepter of chessed was extended to all who join her, and one should say 'Al Ayeles HaShachar' and then pray in their merit.

title.en: The hidden light of the Megillah reading

summary.en: Continuing the Yesod Yosef, the Mashgiach describes a hidden holy world that opens on Purim, whose light lasts the whole day, unlike the moment of 'Ayeh' in Shabbos Kedushah. Because it comes from a concealed place, Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah; 'mikra Megillah' means calling that light down, with great awe at the reading.

title.en: Hashem's Name hidden in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's Name in order means mercy and reversed means judgment; Nisan carries it forward, while Adar is a time of din. Haman's 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li' carries the Name reversed in its final letters, Esther's 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' carries it in its initials, and Hashem gave chassadim to Israel and dinim to Haman. He ends that the Megillah is a flow of chassadim that recurs every year.

catalogTitle: קטרת and שיר השירים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ketores prepared inside the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur expresses the intimate bond of chassan and kallah between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, the same bond that fills Shir HaShirim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the central avodah of Yom Kippur, the ketores, which must be placed on the coals inside the Kodesh HaKodashim. The Tzedukim argued that, as with a king's meal, it should be prepared outside, and the Yerushalmi brings no answer from the Chachamim. The Mashgiach explains that Rosh Hashanah is a day of King and subjects for the whole world, while Yom Kippur belongs to Klal Yisrael alone, as a bride with her beloved. Torah sheba'al peh, the Chachmei Yisrael, is the mistress of the house, and between husband and wife the meal may be prepared in his presence. The Tzedukim, who denied Torah sheba'al peh, could not be answered with one argument. The sense of smell was not damaged by the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as, and the ketores and Shir HaShirim, filled with fragrance, both express this eternal love. He closes with Ne'ilah and with tzedakah as preparation for Yom Kippur.

en: The ketores on Yom Kippur must be put on the fire inside the Kodesh HaKodashim, lifnei Hashem, and not prepared outside and carried in, as the Tzedukim held.
Rosh Hashanah is a day of King and subjects for the whole world, while Yom Kippur is for Klal Yisrael alone, a day of closeness like a bride with her husband.
Between a king and his people the meal is prepared outside, but between husband and wife, when they are alone, it may be prepared in his presence; this answers the Tzedukim's argument.
The Tzedukim denied Torah sheba'al peh and the idea of Klal Yisrael as Hashem's beloved, so the Chachamim could not answer them with a single argument.
The sense of smell was not damaged by the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as, and the ketores, an avodah of smell, represents Hashem's eternal love for Yisrael.
Shir HaShirim, the song of chassan and kallah, is a second Kodesh HaKodashim, and from beginning to end it speaks of fragrance.

candidateTopics: Hashem and Klal Yisrael as chassan and kallah
sense of smell and the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as

title.en: The ketores and the Tzedukim's argument

summary.en: After greeting the guests, the Mashgiach brings that the ketores is the main avodah of Yom Kippur and must be put on the fire inside the Kodesh HaKodashim. He brings the Tzedukim's view, their argument from a king's meal in the Yerushalmi, the story of the Tzeduki Kohen Gadol, and asks why the Chachamim gave no answer.

title.en: King on Rosh Hashanah, beloved on Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Rosh Hashanah, a day for the whole world where Yisrael are subjects of the King, with Yom Kippur, a day for Yisrael alone where they are His beloved. He explains that Torah sheba'al peh is the mistress of the house, and that a queen alone with the king may prepare his food in his presence.

title.en: Yichud in the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yerushalmi that even malachim may not be in the Kodesh HaKodashim when the Kohen Gadol enters, for it is the place of the keruvim, chassan and kallah. He shows from the Shemoneh Esrei of Yom Kippur that only then does Hashem speak to us, and explains that the Tzedukim denied Torah sheba'al peh.

title.en: Why the Chachamim were silent; the sense of smell

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that unlike other disputes with the Tzedukim, here the Chachamim kept silent, because the point rests on a whole outlook the Tzedukim rejected. He then brings from the Bnei Yissaschar that all the senses took part in the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as except smell, the sense of Moshiach.

title.en: Ketores, Shir HaShirim and the name Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ketores expresses Hashem's eternal love for Yisrael, and that Shir HaShirim, the song of chassan and kallah according to Rashi, is a second Kodesh HaKodashim. He explains the hei at the end of the name Shlomo by comparison with Rashi on Avraham's tent, where the kallah comes first.

title.en: Shir HaShirim is full of fragrance

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Shir HaShirim begins and ends with fragrance and returns to it again and again, the one sense untouched by the sin. He concludes that the Tzeduki Kohen Gadol denied Shir HaShirim and the sense of smell, and was punished through his nose.

title.en: Ne'ilah, preparation and tzedakah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Ne'ilah as being closed in alone with Hashem and says that feeling Yom Kippur depends on preparation through teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah. He tells a mashal of travelers who threw off their wagon's wheels to lighten it, applies it to cutting tzedakah in hard times, and closes with brachos.

catalogTitle: יו"ט ליהודים בעלי מדריגה' ומרדכי לא יכרע- היה בטוח בה'' יו"ט של לעתיד לבא' פעמונים בשולי המעיל- דור אחרון

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Shushan Purim as the Yom Tov of the higher levels, Mordechai's refusal to bow as a deeper standard of emunah, and Purim as a foretaste of the complete wiping out of Amalek in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why new Amalekites rose against the Jews in Shushan on the second day and why Esther asked only then for Haman's ten sons to be hanged. He answers that Purim reaches the lowest Jews while Shushan Purim belongs to the higher ones, the walled-city Jews tied to Jerusalem; what is no sin for one is a sin for another, so finer Amalekites and the ten sons, the soul's ten powers, are destroyed on the second day. He then reads the Targum on Mordechai's refusal to bow to Haman and resolves its contradiction with the Divrei Yoel: Avraham's tractate Avodah Zarah had 400 chapters, and for Mordechai believing that Haman provides one's bread is idolatry. Every Jew, he says, must know this truth and never despair. Turning to Megillah 7a, he explains that the Megillah holds the light of Moshiach, links Shushan Purim to a bris milah, and closes with Esther's wish that the Yom Tov bind the Jews of the last generation to Jerusalem.

en: Purim reaches down to the simplest Jews, while Shushan Purim is the Yom Tov of the higher levels, the walled-city Jews connected to Jerusalem.
Each Jew is judged by his level: what is permitted for one is a sin for a higher one, so there are Amalekites that count as Amalek only for the higher Jew.
Haman attacks the basic belief in Divine providence that every Jew has, while his ten sons are the soul's ten powers, which only the Shushan Purim Jew is expected to uproot.
For Mordechai, believing that one must bow to Haman because he controls one's funding is itself avodah zarah, a chapter in a higher tractate of Avodah Zarah.
Every Jew must know that wealth and honor come only from Hashem, and must not despair over his low state, just as Jerusalem will be rebuilt.
Amalek was written in Scripture only three times because it was never fully destroyed; the Megillah carries the light of Moshiach and lets Jews grow used to it.

title.en: Amalek's brazenness and the second day

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Amalek's brazenness, which made Haman's descendants reveal themselves by rising against the Jews. He asks why new Amalekites appeared in Shushan on the second day and why Esther asked only then for Haman's ten sons to be hanged.

title.en: Purim for the low, Shushan Purim for the high

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim reaches the lowest Jews while Shushan Purim belongs to the walled-city Jews tied to Jerusalem. He brings the Targum Sheni that Mordechai came to Shushan only to raise Esther, because his light could be revealed only in a place of hiddenness.

title.en: Each by his level, and finer Amalekites

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that what is permitted for one Jew is a sin for a higher one, and so there are finer Amalekites who count as Amalek only for the higher Jew; these sprang up on the second day. He connects Shushan with Jerusalem through the Shushan gate of the Temple Mount.

title.en: Esther and Shoshanah; rejoicing together

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Esther, hiddenness, with Shoshanah, the rose whose beauty is revealed. He says both days must be kept: Jews outside rejoice with the higher Jews tied to Mordechai, and the Jews of Jerusalem rejoice with the Jews of exile.

title.en: Haman, his ten sons, and inner Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman attacks the basic emunah in Divine providence that every Jew has, while his ten sons are the soul's ten powers, which the Shushan Purim Jew must uproot. He notes that where inner Torah took hold, among the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples, Shushan Purim became a real Yom Tov, and in the days of Moshiach it will spread to the whole world.

title.en: The Targum on Mordechai's refusal to bow

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Megillah with the Targum: Mordechai bowed neither to the idol nor to Haman, who had sold himself to him for a loaf of bread. Later the Jews complain, and Mordechai answers that Haman wore images on his garment; the Mashgiach points out the contradiction and asks why Mordechai's Sanhedrin sat at the king's gate.

title.en: Avraham's 400 chapters of Avodah Zarah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Yoel on the Gemara that Avraham's tractate Avodah Zarah had 400 chapters while ours has five: idolatry has many levels, and what is not idolatry for a simple person is idolatry for a greater one. He insists the Targum's contradiction cannot be dismissed as differing midrashim.

title.en: The king's funds and Mordechai's emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that Achashverosh supported religions, so Mordechai's Sanhedrin, funded by the king, sat at the king's gate, and Haman administered all the funds. Everyone bowed to Haman, but Mordechai stood firm in emunah that wealth and honor come from Hashem, and the Jews complained that his refusal brought the decree.

title.en: Haman's garment: idolatry from front and back

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Mordechai's answer through the Divrei Yoel: believing one must bow to Haman because he provides one's bread is idolatry on a higher level, and even forgetting for a moment that Hashem rules is the image 'from behind'. Mordechai hinted that he feeds Haman, since all blessing comes first to Israel.

title.en: Knowing the truth, and the dance

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Jews fell silent because they understood: even one not on Mordechai's level must know the truth and recall it in hard moments, when tempted to flatter whoever seems to give his livelihood. He compares this to dancing at a simcha, when a person jumps above his own height though he will come down again.

title.en: Every Jewish heart is Jerusalem

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Shushan Purim means to Jews outside Jerusalem and answers that every Jewish heart is Jerusalem. A Jew who feels he wasted Purim should remember that ruined Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and so will he; he closes with 'layehudim haysah orah' and a blessing that the beauty of a Jew be revealed.

title.en: 'Three and not four': the Megillah's place

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara in Megillah where Esther asks to be written for generations and the Sages answer that Amalek is written three times and not four, and with the dispute whether Esther defiles the hands. He explains the 24 holy books as the 24 ornaments of the bride, the Shechinah, each prophet bringing down an ornament already prepared in heaven.

title.en: The light of Moshiach in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Likkutei Torah of Chernobyl that the Megillah holds the light of Moshiach, given so that Jews can grow used to that great light. Purim will remain when other festivals are annulled because its essence is the wiping out of Amalek, the preparation for Moshiach; until that is complete the Megillah's full holiness is still 'in heaven'.

title.en: The seudah of Shushan Purim as a bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Megillah needs the laws of holy writings only as an object of the mitzvah on Purim. He explains that a bris milah, like Purim, gives a glimmer of the days of Moshiach as the orlah is removed and the holy point is revealed, so the seudah of Shushan Purim is a seudas bris milah.

title.en: Blessing for the bris; why only three times

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the newly circumcised child, whose bris falls on Shushan Purim, and all present. He then returns to 'three and not four': Amalek was only weakened by Yehoshua, Shaul left Agag, and in the Megillah too Hashem's name is hidden, so the Sages hesitated to write it until they found it in a passuk.

title.en: Bells on the hem: Esther's Yom Tov for the last generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bells and pomegranates on the hem of the Kohen Gadol's robe hint at the last generations, the simple Jews 'full of mitzvos like a pomegranate'. Esther could not ask Achashverosh for a Yom Tov for Jerusalem, so she asked for Shushan, knowing Shushan would vanish while Jerusalem remains; the day binds the last generation to Jerusalem.

catalogTitle: גדולת מרדכי. גראמען (מר' שלמה לעזער שליט"א)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Mordechai, whom the Gemara ranks lower for leaving Torah study to save lives, was in truth the head of all tzaddikim and the Moshe of his generation, whose bond with Torah was never broken.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Mordechai, listed after four men in one passuk and after five in another, dropped in rank once he left Torah study for public affairs, from which Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives. He asks why, then, only some of the Sanhedrin separated from him, and shows Mordechai's stature: the Gemara finds him in the Torah as mor dror, the Midrash calls him head of all tzaddikim, and the Zohar calls him the soul of Moshe. The greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov and the Avos, stay bound to Torah even in worldly affairs. The Gemara and Ezra wrote by pshat, each tzaddik according to his soul's root; the minority of the Sanhedrin were souls of pshat, like the Beis Yosef. Mordechai is mor dror, misjudged by some, and every level is true. At the end come grammen by another speaker.

en: From Mordechai's lower ranking in the second passuk, the Gemara learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives.
Mordechai is the head of all tzaddikim and the soul of Moshe Rabbeinu, and on Purim his great light comes down into the world.
The greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov at Lavan's house and the Avos, can be busy with worldly matters while their whole occupation remains Torah.
Every tzaddik writes according to the root of his soul, so Ezra's placing of Mordechai reflects Ezra's level of understanding.
The minority of the Sanhedrin who separated from Mordechai were souls of pshat, while the majority understood that he never left the depths of Torah.
Opposing views of a tzaddik can each be true on its own level, as the Chiddushei HaRim says of the Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov bowing to Esav.

title.en: Mordechai's lower ranking and Torah versus saving lives

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Mordechai is listed after four men in one passuk and after five in another, because he became the king's second and could no longer learn as before; from here Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives. He raises the difficulty that saving a life overrides the whole Torah, and asks why Mordechai's situation should show a weakness in his Torah.

title.en: Mordechai, head of all tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the rest of the Sanhedrin did not separate from Mordechai, and shows his stature: the Gemara finds him in the Torah as mor dror, the Midrash calls him head of all tzaddikim, and the Zohar says he was the soul of Moshe. He explains that the greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov tending Lavan's sheep and the Avos, never interrupted their bond with Hashem in worldly affairs, and that Mordechai's way was hidden.

title.en: Each tzaddik writes by his soul's root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Gemara speaks by pshat. With the Zohar and the Rema MiFano on Hadar, the eighth king, whose death the Torah does not record but Ezra's pesukim do, he shows that each tzaddik writes by his soul's root, so Ezra's ranking of Mordechai reflects Ezra's level. Moshe too did not truly die, and Haman, who knew Moshe died in Adar but not that he was born in Adar, did not know that Mordechai was the Moshe of his generation.

title.en: The minority of the Sanhedrin: souls of pshat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the minority of the Sanhedrin who separated were souls of pshat, which does not make them smaller, just as the Arizal told the Beis Yosef that his root was teaching halachah. The majority understood that Mordechai, like the Avos, never left the depths of Torah; he adds a hint from the initials of the names in the passuk, whose shin alludes to the three Avos.

title.en: Mor dror, and every level is true

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute of the Rambam and the Raavad over musk, mor dror, and says Mordechai is like it: some cannot understand him and judge him unfit, and mor dror equals in gematria that Moshe was born on the seventh of Adar. With the Chiddushei HaRim on Yaakov bowing to Esav he explains that each level is true, and closes that the Megillah ends with Mordechai seeking the good of his people, as in every generation Mordechai brings salvation to Jews.

title.en: Announcements and grammen on doubled words

summary.en: Another speaker makes announcements, then begins rhymed Purim grammen asking why words are doubled in the Megillah and in tefillah.

title.en: Grammen: the tale of the new chassid

summary.en: The grammen continue with a rhymed tale about a simple chassid brought to Vizhnitz and the passages he wished to skip in davening.

title.en: Grammen: threefold mercy and Moshiach

summary.en: The grammen conclude with rhymes on remembering the Creator, His mercy and the coming of Moshiach, with a closing appeal for tzedakah.
